articles.title_orig: From high-flying AI stocks to tariff-hit alcohol companies, the midterms shook up Wall Street
articles.title_zh: From high-flying AI stocks to tariff-hit alcohol companies, the midterms shook up Wall Street
articles.content_orig:
Asian and European markets follow US tech rout with many analysts predicting more waves of selling to come
European and Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday after the Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterms triggered a rout in US tech stocks a day earlier.
A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stock markets on Friday. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market was, at one stage, poised for its worst day since March.
The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down as much as 254 points, or 2.35%, at 10,528 points during a wave of selling in morning trading. But by the close of the day it had clawed back some of its losses to be down 1%, helped by a rise in US stocks when Wall Street reopened.
Germany’s Dax index fell by 2%, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 0.8% and Spain’s Ibex lost 0.6%.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe .
“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”
However, there were signs of easing jitters on Wall Street on Friday, where tech stocks rose, lifting the S&P 500 share index by 0.3% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq closed up 1% – which only recovered a portion of their previous day’s losses.
That followed a stronger-than-expected employment report that showed the US economy added 165,000 new jobs in October, pulling the unemployment rate down to 4.1%.
On Thursday, the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.
Chip stocks led the slump on Thursday, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by more than 60% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.
The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 6.5%.
“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets.
“[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’”
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Yesterday’s [Thursday’s] brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come.
after newsletter promotion
“Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.”
However, despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year. The Nasdaq Composite index remains up 6.35% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak.
The FTSE 100 has gained almost 7.5% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July.
Mohit Kumar, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said that while he did not expect a quick rebound from Thursday’s losses in the US, he also did not believe it marked the “start of the unwind of the AI trade”.
He said: “AI investment has been a key driver of US growth and we do not see the Democrats as giving up on this growth engine. Datacentres and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move on to other states or outside the country.”
Stock market tremors have also hit the London Metal Exchange, with copper poised for its biggest weekly fall since March.
Benchmark three-month copper, a key metal used in the semiconductor, electronics and automotive industry, has dropped 0.61%, leaving it positioned for a 2.79% fall this week.
Craig Lang, a principal analyst at the consultancy CRU, said the price of copper was increasingly influenced by the AI market and “sentiment towards datacentre expansion”.

articles.content_orig:
Echoing Obama’s 2016 visit, the Apec meeting will show whether Trump can broker enduring agreements with Beijing
Following the Republicans’ loss of both chambers of the US Congress in the midterm elections on Tuesday – a drubbing that reached deep into historically red states – Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in two weeks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen. It will be their third face-to-face meeting this year.

articles.title_orig: After the US midterm rout of Trumpism, the world struggles to trust America again
articles.title_zh: After the US midterm rout of Trumpism, the world struggles to trust America again
articles.content_orig:
The US midterm elections could have consequences far beyond the country’s borders. President Donald Trump has spent nearly two years overturning decades of American foreign policy, unsettling allies and adversaries alike. Now, both are watching to see how an electoral setback at home will shape his actions abroad.
For Iran, Israel and Ukraine, the stakes go well beyond who controls Congress. The result could influence whether Trump pursues a deal with Tehran or more war, how much Washington’s longstanding support for Israel erodes, and how hard he pushes Kyiv to accept terms to end Russia’s war.
Democrats will have new tools to challenge Trump. But he still has considerable freedom to act abroad, leaving world leaders with a question: Will defeat make him more willing to compromise, or more determined to get his way?
Here’s how the vote could impact Washington’s most pressing foreign policy concerns:
Iran is celebrating Trump’s midterm setback, but it is bracing for what comes next: a possible new US strike or a fresh push for a deal.
Trump admitted in a call with Fox News that the war in Iran was partly to blame for the Republicans’ losses but Vice President JD Vance was more explicit, saying in a lengthy X post Wednesday that “the reason we lost is the war.”
After eight months of striking the region’s economic lifelines to turn American voters against the war, Tehran has hailed the Republican loss as a public verdict on it. Trump acknowledged that war-driven price hikes played a role.
“If the US government betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has led negotiations with the US, wrote on X.
Tehran is not betting on a change of course in Washington. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said anyone who believes the results will shift US policy is “deeply mistaken,” and officials say Iran’s strategy doesn’t hinge on American elections as they prepare for more war while intensifying diplomacy.
The risk of escalation is real. Reports that Trump might order new, more intense strikes are fueling anxiety across the region, and Tehran has warned that its retaliation would be much wider in scope than in earlier rounds. This week, Trump told some journalists he is considering striking Iran hard, and others that he has no immediate plans to escalate.
Top Republicans blame Iran war for midterm results
“The Iran war has become a political albatross around his neck, leaving (Trump) with a stark choice: cut a face-saving deal and declare victory, or double down militarily to reclaim the initiative,” Ali Vaez of International Crisis Group told CNN. “The danger is that a president weakened at the ballot box may seek redemption on the battlefield.”
Diplomacy offers another path. Talks that stagnated over the summer have picked up in the past week, with Tehran sending officials to Qatari mediators who are circulating proposals with Washington. Before the vote, Iran offered to open the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Trump agreed to its seven conditions.
Sanam Vakil of Chatham House said Iran’s leadership “might feel vindicated,” but that “does not necessarily solve their problems.” Trump needs a diplomatic victory yet may be reluctant to appear weak, she said, while Tehran could read his setback as a chance to demand greater concessions. She expects intensified diplomacy alongside military threats, with an interim Strait of Hormuz deal “more realistic” than a comprehensive one.
In Israel, the election day announcement that Trump would abruptly cut off US military aid to the country was the first surprise. The results, with Democrats sweeping both chambers of Congress in what has been called a “blue tsunami,” are a five-alarm fire in Israel.
Bipartisan support for Israel in the US had already been eroding, with Democrats outraged at Israel over the death toll in the Gaza war and a growing number of Republicans believing the US has given it too much support.
“The only bipartisan issue right now is criticism of Israel,” said Michael Oren, a former Israeli ambassador to the US. “It’s an organizing principle for the Democratic Party,” he told CNN. “And it’s becoming an organizing principle for much of the Republican Party.”
Oren said the end of US aid is just the beginning of a process that has only started to play out. He said it’s conceivable that the US could end intelligence sharing with Israel and the joint development of critical military systems, such as the vaunted Iron Dome aerial defense system. He also pointed to the United Nations Security Council, where Republican and Democratic presidents have protected Israel with the US veto.
“We are at the end of an era,” he said.
Trump’s Election Day bombshell on Israel points to historic shift in US politics
Yaakov Katz, a former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, warned there is more to come. “What Trump announced about the military aid yesterday is just the tip of the iceberg of what can change – arms sales could be blocked, sanctions will be proposed and joint economic programs defunded,” he said on X.
The anti-Israel sentiment only hardened during the Iran war, with segments of the US electorate viewing the joint US-Israel strikes as a war that Netanyahu sold to Trump. Even now, Netanyahu has been pushing to resume strikes on Iran, which would reignite a war that drove gas prices and the cost of living higher and contributed to Republicans’ devastating midterm performance.
Netanyahu also faces turmoil at home. In elections a week before the midterms, he lost his majority in parliament, but his main rival, former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, does not have an outright majority and would likely need to cooperate with Arab parties, who saw record turnout.
Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats party, warned that Israel “does not have time to waste” in replacing Netanyahu and leading the country away from sanctions and isolation.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky is hoping the the “blue wave” will bolster American support for its defense against Russia’s war.
“I am also grateful to the Republicans, but the Democrats speak very clearly about supporting Ukraine and providing assistance to Ukraine,” Zelensky said in comments provided in German by broadcaster ZDF, ahead of the telecast of the interview, according to Reuters.
“They speak about renewing the connection between the United States and Europe… Therefore, there is hope that a balance of power will emerge and that we will receive more support.”
He added: “If Congress now speaks of strong financial support or military assistance, as Europe is doing and demonstrating today, then that will be something positive that will have an impact on Putin.”
For weeks, President Volodymyr Zelensky’s relationship with Trump has been in freefall. Trump has demanded Zelensky be replaced; courted energy deals to benefit Russia; and watched as Ukraine’s tech and intel dependencies on the US were inexplicably thwarted. And so Kyiv was forced to take a position early: wait, with urgency, for a post-Trump world.
And when it began to dawn on Wednesday, there was little official comment from Kyiv at first, Zelensky perhaps happy for the memes of him, sat with a beer and popcorn in front of the mid-term TV coverage, to do the job for him.
A deputy in his office, Sergiy Kyslytsia, pledged on Ukrainian TV that the country would continue to “develop genuine, normal and stable relations” with whoever is in office, seek Patriot interceptors, and navigate both a new Congress and the likely flurry of executive orders that may try to obviate it.
But there can be no disguising that a crestfallen Trump, and the slow clock now loudly ticking on his worldview and presidency, is in Kyiv’s favour. articles.title_orig: Berkshire Hathaway’s Operating Earnings Fall, Buybacks Rise
articles.title_zh: Berkshire Hathaway’s Operating Earnings Fall, Buybacks Rise
articles.content_orig:
Berkshire Hathaway said Saturday it accelerated its share repurchases during the third quarter, as operating and overall profits took a hit.
The Greg Abel-led conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock. That's more than double the $4.5 billion repurchased in the second quarter and brings the company's total buybacks for 2026 to about $14.4 billion.
The sharp increase came as Berkshire's operating earnings — those from wholly-owned businesses — fell year over year, as profits from its insurance business pulled back.
Berkshire operating profits totaled $12.705 billion, down 5.8% from $13.485 billion in the year-earlier period. Insurance underwriting tumbled 43% year on year to $1.352 billion, while insurance investment income declined 14% to $2.734 billion. Berkshire's railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses all saw earnings grow year over year.
The company's overall earnings, which include Berkshire's sprawling stock market portfolio, also dropped 28% in the third quarter to $22.112 billion from $30.796 billion a year prior. Investment gains for the company fell nearly 50% to $9.407 billion.
Despite the earnings pullback, Berkshire stock has outperformed recently amid a massive rotation out of technology stocks. Class A shares are up more than 12% over the past month, while the S&P 500 has dropped 5.5% in that time. Year to date, Berkshire has gained 13%, while the broad market index is up just 7.8%.
Berkshire's five largest equity holdings remained the same in the third quarter: Alphabet , American Express , Apple , Bank of America and Coca-Cola .
Berkshire's cash hoard also grew 3% in the third quarter $377.435 billion from $365.514 billion in the second quarter. However, excluding rail and utility cash along with T-bill payables, the conglomerate's cash holdings totaled $352.3 billion, down 1.9% quarter over quarter.
— CNBC's Alex Crippen contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO meets AI backlash after midterms show stinging rebuke of data centers
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO meets AI backlash after midterms show stinging rebuke of data centers
articles.content_orig:
Americans were unequivocal at the ballot box this week as they expressed disdain for tech billionaires and mistrust of artificial intelligence. With that backdrop, Anthropic is about to try to go public.
The AI company is gearing up for a potentially historic IPO, likely targeting mid-November for its Nasdaq debut. CNBC reported on Friday that Anthropic investors see the company aiming for a valuation of $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion, down from a target of $2 trillion that had been floated in recent months.
From Wall Street to Main Street, it's becoming a tougher environment for Anthropic. The Nasdaq on Thursday suffered its steepest drop in 19 months, and it's down to start November after October marked its worst month since March 2025. Chipmakers and neoclouds, the companies most closely tied to the AI buildout, are getting hit the hardest.
Voters rebuked AI in Tuesday's midterm elections, while sending Democrats to sweeping congressional victories across the country. Candidates who advocated for more stringent AI regulation won handily in states like Michigan, Ohio, Texas and Georgia, which will all now have Democratic governors, and local communities opposed data center-related ballot measures in 40 out of 41 cases .
More than half of voters said AI data centers were a "crucial" or "major factor" in who they supported for Congress, according to an exit poll from NBC News.
"People don't want a data center going near them if it's just going to house AI that's going to help a big tech company profit," Maura Austin, a behavioral scientist at the University of Virginia, told CNBC. "What Anthropic is doing when they're going public with such a high valuation is they're really leaning into that big tech, billionaire kind of caricature. I expect that's not going to go well with the public."
Anthropic has long tried to position itself as a safety-conscious company that takes AI's potential risks and benefits seriously. CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company alongside a handful of researchers who defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.
The company's enterprise focus has helped it avoid becoming the public face of AI, leaving that distinction to OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman . But with Anthropic poised to become the first pure-play AI company to hit the public market, minting a number of new billionaires and many more millionaires in the process, a heightened level of scrutiny is coming.
"Being a public company, just that by itself pushes you in the limelight," Reena Aggarwal, a professor of finance at Georgetown University, said in an interview. "And then AI is such a hot-button issue that Anthropic will be in the limelight even more."
Matt Kennedy, a senior IPO market strategist at Renaissance Capital, said that's not necessarily a bad thing for Anthropic.
Public markets force greater transparency, he said, and the company could attract new users through its debut. And since AI has become such a mainstream conversation topic, several private companies are already household names.
"I would say that a public company does not deserve more criticisms than a comparable private company," Kennedy said. "So Anthropic should not be put in a harsher public spotlight than OpenAI just because it's public."
Anthropic declined to comment.
AI backlash accelerated over the summer after a series of high-profile safety and security incidents rattled the public. As concerns mounted, the debate over data centers intensified, while tech's hyperscalers  simultaneously boosted their forecasts for capital expenditures, each reaching into the hundreds of billions of dollars.
Anthropic and OpenAI depend on state-of-the-art data centers to train models and serve customers, and they're trying to build out capacity as quickly as possible to meet demand. Anthropic said in an amended IPO prospectus this week that it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion , "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."
Americans grappling with inflation and stubbornly high gas prices have grown worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, a proposed data center in their backyard became the physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy toward AI.
In the risk factors section of its prospectus , Anthropic said opposition to data center development has become more organized across jurisdictions, and that the company's public profile could draw particular scrutiny to projects associated with it.
Nicole Greene, an analyst at Gartner, said she expects that Anthropic's executives have long been prepared to contend with AI backlash, especially given the disruptive nature of the technology.
"There's going to be big emotions," Greene told CNBC. "With big emotions and feelings — fear and excitement — comes heightened scrutiny."
Amodei acknowledged the souring sentiment around AI in a post on X in August. He said it's the result of a "crisis of trust," and that people believe companies, the government and the tech industry are always "cooking up some new way to screw them over."
Rebuilding public confidence is going to be an uphill battle as the company begins providing quarterly financial updates.
The University of Southern California published a survey on Monday that found that 71% of respondents don't trust big tech companies to act in society's best interest "at all" around data center development.
"Once you've lost trust, it's hard to gain it back," Wändi Bruine de Bruin, a professor at the University of Southern California's Schaeffer Institute, said in an interview. "The numbers are not good."

articles.title_orig: Berkshire shares surge as Wall Street swoons amid AI fears
articles.title_zh: Berkshire shares surge as Wall Street swoons amid AI fears
articles.content_orig:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire Hathaway shares roared past the S&P 500 index this week as investors moved money away from slumping tech stocks and moved into what appears to be the relative safety of a traditional conglomerate with relatively little exposure to artificial intelligence amid fears massive spending on data centers won't pay off .
One month ago, Berkshire's widely held B shares were underperforming the S&P by 13.6 percentage points for the year.
With help from three more record-high closes this week, Berkshire is now 5.8 percentage points ahead of the benchmark.
Berkshire more than doubled its share repurchases last quarter to $9.6 billion, while operating earnings declined slightly, the company said on Saturday .
Berkshire was up more than 5% this week while the S&P fell almost 2.7%.
The contrast is even sharper with the Nasdaq Composite , which fell 3.4% on the week.
Thursday's especially heavy tech selling pushed the index down more than 10% below its most recent high in what is commonly referred to as a " correction ," but it did make up some of its lost ground Friday .
Two weeks ago, Berkshire's share prices completely erased all of the roughly 15% drop they suffered in the three months following Warren Buffett's surprise announcement at the 2025 shareholders meeting that he would step down as CEO at the end of that year.
Now they are up 6% from the record high closes they hit the Friday before Buffett's revelation on May 3, 2025.
Berkshire is not completely removed from the convulsions around AI.
Abel told us in early September he sees a " significant opportunity " ahead for Berkshire Hathaway Energy to provide electricity to data centers.
He also expected Berkshire would benefit from its big bet on Google parent Alphabet , saying he and Warren Buffett knew AI was "going to have a significant impact on America and businesses," and " we saw Google as a significant player . "
Now that investment is getting negative reviews this week as the stock slumps along with other companies related to AI.
As of the end of June, Berkshire reported it owned almost 106 million shares of Alphabet, including 28.6 million shares it bought directly from the company in June: $5 billion of its Class A shares (GOOGL) for $351.81 each and another $5 billion of Class C shares (GOOG) for $348.20 each.
They are around $284 per share now.
It bought another $7 billion of Alphabet shares on the open market during the second quarter, adding to the position it started building in last year's third quarter, an investment initiated by Warren Buffett .
Bloomberg suggests that "with cracks in the AI trade starting to show, Berkshire's sudden push [into AI] may appear ill-timed."
On June 30, the position had a market value of $37.8 billion and it was the third largest equity holding in Berkshire's portfolio.
Since then both the Class A and Class C shares have dropped by around 20% and the stake is now valued at $30.2 billion , falling behind Coca-Cola's $38.3 billion to the portfolio's #4 position.
(In just over a week, we'll find out whether Berkshire made any changes to its Alphabet position during the third quarter ending September 30.)
Bloomberg quotes CFRA Research analyst Cathy Seifert as saying, "I do think that part of this may be a conscious decision to increase their exposure. One has to ask the question though, is it a little late?"
But the article notes that "for dedicated value investors and longtime Berkshire observers, such jitters may not really matter," with Keefe Bruyette & Woods analyst Meyer Shields saying Abel probably sees bets on AI as a long-term wager on the technology's potential, in keeping with the "conservatism that you would expect at Berkshire Hathaway."
At Barron's , however, Andrew Bary sees what he estimates is a $3 billion loss on Alphabet as part of a "disappointing" long-term trend in Berkshire's stock choices
"The company hasn't created much value from stock picking during the current decade" even though the "S&P 500 has returned 150% since the end of 2019 and tech stocks have quadrupled."
While Berkshire's investments in five Japanese "trading houses ," Chevron , and Chubb have done well, "there have been plenty of losers or simply mediocre investments that have been closed out."
He cites Verizon , HP , Paramount (now Skydance) , General Motors , Constellation Brands , and Pool .
While he estimates Berkshire's Occidental Petroleum investment is up about 20% from what it paid, OXY is "far behind most energy stocks" amid this year's big increase in crude prices.
Bary also lists stocks that have continued to rise in price after Berkshire cut its stakes, with Apple being the worst offender.
That stake has been reduced by 75% since 2023 at what Bary calculates is an average selling price around $200 per share, well below AAPL's current $342.
Despite those sales, Apple is Berkshire's largest equity holding with a market value of $78 billion . The stock is up 1200% since Berkshire started buying it at the beginning of 2016, at a time when many thought the company had already seen its best days.
Bary thinks Abel will probably keep Berkshire's core equity investments but may concentrate more on his strengths going forward: improving Berkshire's operating companies and making new acquisitions.
His conclusion: "Barring a market rout, equity investing may not be central to Berkshire anymore.
"And if any new Berkshire holdings are revealed soon, it may not be a good idea to buy them. The record hasn't been great."
Berkshire Hathaway's disclosure that it had made a relatively small $27 million addition to its $4.1 billion Sirius XM position helped fuel an ongoing rally that lifted the satellite radio company's shares to a 52-week high this week.
On Thursday morning last week, Sirius XM reported a 14% increase in its Q3 free cash flow, 5,000 more self-pay subscribers, and it raised its 2026 full-year financial guidance.
The stock ended 4.9% higher that day at $28.67.
On Friday, Monday, and Tuesday, Berkshire bought more than 924 thousand shares at an average price of $29.10 as the stock continued to gain ground, ending Tuesday at $30.80.
Berkshire disclosed the buys late Tuesday evening, apparently helping to fuel an additional 8.4% gain as the stock closed at $33.40 on Wednesday.
It hit a 52-week intraday high of $33.76 on Thursday but finished lower Friday at $32.40.
Overall, Sirius XM is up 18.6% since the earnings release and has gained 62.0% so far this year.
It's the first addition to Berkshire's stake since late-July and early-August last year.
In 2025, it bought a total of 7.3 million shares at an average price of $21.86.
The position is likely one of portfolio manager Ted Weschler's stocks.
Pacific Power, a unit of Berkshire Hathaway's PacifiCorp, is asking California regulators for a 57% rate increase that would raise the typical residential electric bill by $120 a month.
The Wall Street Journal calls it a "stunning request even in an era of rising electricity costs."
The utility says the hike would be partially offset by a 14% decrease taking effect on January 1.
A lot of the $103 million that would be generated by the increase is already being spent on efforts to make power equipment in the sparsely populated and heavily wooded area more resistant to wildfires.
The utility is facing around $637 million in liability claims for fires in 2020 and 2022.
This week, Reuters reports , Oregon's Supreme Court heard arguments on whether to revive a jury verdict that could expose PacifiCorp "to tens of billions of dollars of potential damages over its role in four Oregon wildfires in 2020."

articles.title_orig: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
articles.content_orig:
Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.
Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.
Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.
The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
Zelensky wrote on Telegram that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".
Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.
"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.
"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."
In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.
The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.
Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.
The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.
She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.
She thanked both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.
Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire , which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.
"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.
Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhzhia , with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.
Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.
He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.
"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."
Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.
Additional reporting by Daniel Wittenberg

articles.title_orig: Governor-Elect of Texas Announces Plans to Control Elon Musk
articles.title_zh: Governor-Elect of Texas Announces Plans to Control Elon Musk
articles.content_orig:
The governor-elect of Texas Gina Hinojosa made it clear on the campaign trail that she would work to rein in data centers and billionaire tech barons. And now that she’s headed into office, that means playing hardball with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
“We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies, but it has to be on our terms,” Hinojosa said Thursday in an interview with CNN , as quoted by Bloomberg . “It cannot be just running over the people of Texas, and that’s what changes now that I will be governor.”
A central part of Hinojosa’s campaign was demanding an immediate moratorium on new data center construction until lawmakers have established tighter regulations and stronger protections for local communities.
In the Thursday interview, Hinojosa reiterated her commitment to placing more stringent regulations on data centers by saying she would “balance” it with keeping Texas a business-friendly state.
She also shared that she’s already making moves to crack down on Musk. Amid speculation that Texas officials have been considering a sale of state park land to SpaceX, Hinojosa said she spoke to the head of the Texas Parks & Wildlife Department to “request that no action be taken,” per Bloomberg .
“It is such an important resource,” she told reporters in Austin, hours before the CNN interview.
Wall Street and the AI industry are watching Hinojosa closely, as Texas has become the nucleus of the data center boom. Over a quarter of the US’s planned data center capacity resides in the state.
Musk is deeply invested in the state, having relocated his companies SpaceX and Tesla there from California. He’s also reportedly exploring sites to build another large data center in Texas , to add to the controversial “Colossus” facilities he operates in Greater Memphis. That’s not to mention the quarter of a billion dollars he poured into the midterms to support Republican candidates.
Of course, Musk could simply do what many think is impossible — or at least economically infeasible — and ditch terrestrial AI instrastructure altogether.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote on X , following the brutal election loss.

articles.title_orig: British soldier ignored order to pull his SIM card, then got blackmailed
articles.title_zh: British soldier ignored order to pull his SIM card, then got blackmailed
articles.content_orig:
An Estonian newspaper recently revealed that a British soldier disobeyed a direct order to remove the SIM card from his cellphone before being deployed to a part of Estonia, approximately 90 miles west of the Russian border.
As a result of his refusal to engage in this element of operational security (opsec), the soldier, Daniel Barton-Kennedy, had his phone hacked, and nude photos of himself were stolen and used as blackmail against him.
Eventually, Barton-Kennedy was court-martialed for disobeying a lawful command, pled guilty, was reduced in rank, and ordered to serve 10 months in detention.
According to a 21-page British appeals court document shared with Ars Technica by Eesti Ekspress, the Estonian newspaper that first reported on this saga, the story begins in January 2026.
At the time, Barton-Kennedy was a corporal, with over seven years of service, serving in the 1st Battalion of the Duke of Lancaster Regiment of the British Army.
His unit was deployed to participate in “Exercise Eastern Warrior” in Tapa, Estonia, roughly halfway between Tallinn, the capital city, and the Estonia-Russia border.
While in the United Kingdom, on January 7, Barton-Kennedy, along with other members of his unit, were briefed on their orders and given specific instructions to “remove SIM cards and switch off location settings and to use a trusted virtual private network on all personal electronic devices.”
Once the unit arrived in Estonia, days later, they were given further briefings and reminders of this policy. Despite this, Barton-Kennedy ignored the instruction.
On January 19, Barton-Kennedy informed his platoon commander that he had received a message “from an unknown party who had acquired nude photographs of him from the photo section of his mobile phone and had identified him on social media.”
Barton-Kennedy initially acquiesced to paying the attacker 100 British pounds ($133) but balked when he was asked to pay 250 British pounds ($333), and only then informed his platoon commander what had happened.
Eventually, Barton-Kennedy was court-martialed and pled guilty at a hearing on July 30.
During that process, according to the court filing, Barton-Kennedy understood the orders that were given to him at the time, but asked the court to “consider the personal circumstances” that he faced at the time. Without his phone, he told the court, he could not reach his daughter on her birthday, nor his pregnant partner.
In a written statement, Barton-Kennedy said he was stunned when he received the first blackmail message.
“Despite still being in a state of shock and uncertainty, I recognised that I had a duty to report the compromise without any further delay,” he wrote.
Additionally, he said that he “deeply regrets” the incident and added that serving in the British Army “has been one of the greatest privileges of my life.”
Barton-Kennedy appealed the sentence, which was denied in August 2026.
In response to an inquiry for comment, Lt. Col. EP Mackie, a British Army spokesperson, told Ars in a statement that the security measures imposed are meant to protect the safety of military personnel.
“Any breaches of Army security measures that might compromise personal safeguarding or operational security will be dealt with swiftly, and offending personnel can expect uncompromising disciplinary action,” he wrote.

articles.title_orig: ‘Very strange, very sad’: Paraguay bank collapse fells a presidency and leaves millions broke
articles.title_zh: ‘Very strange, very sad’: Paraguay bank collapse fells a presidency and leaves millions broke
articles.content_orig:
Santiago Peña’s links to Ueno Bank scrutinized after crisis led to his house arrest and froze millions of bank accounts
Pedro Volpe had just woken up last Tuesday when he saw a message from a friend asking whether his bank account was down, too.
It was a day after payday, and Volpe, 50, a writer and lawyer, opened his banking app and panicked: he could not even see his balance.
Volpe was among nearly 3 million Paraguayans, about 60% of the country’s adult population, whose accounts had been frozen overnight. All were customers of Ueno Bank, a digital lender that aggressively expanded across the South American country in recent years, and which, on Monday night, the central bank ordered into resolution over insolvency.
Ueno is at the centre of a political and economic crisis that has brought Paraguay’s banking system to the brink of collapse. On Friday, it led to the impeachment and house arrest of the rightwing president, Santiago Peña.
Peña had resigned the day before in a vain attempt to retain the special jurisdiction afforded to former presidents – who, under the constitution, become senators for life. Lawmakers stripped him of the seat anyway, meaning Peña will face criminal proceedings in the ordinary courts.
In just a few days, he went from being a market favourite among Latin American presidents and one of Donald Trump’s key allies in the region to facing fierce mass protests, being voted out and placed under house arrest.
The now former president is the subject of an investigation by the public prosecutor’s office over alleged favouritism towards Ueno, which, in just a few years since Peña took office in 2023, went from an obscure digital lender to the bank of choice for most Paraguayans.
“It was very easy to use and to open an account,” said Volpe, recalling that everything could be done quickly on a mobile phone. The bank also offered far more generous investment returns than its competitors did.
“Now I’m having to work miracles to pay my bills,” added Volpe. “A lot of people can’t even afford basic everyday things like food; luckily, I still had some money saved elsewhere, but that has only got me this far. I don’t know what I’ll do next week.”
Ueno was so popular – sponsoring the national football team, the league and the country’s biggest football clubs – and served such a large share of the population that businesses have already reported an overall fall in sales of up to 80% this week. Media outlets belonging to the same financial group as the bank had their operations suspended, including radio stations and the century-old newspaper La Tribuna .
The impact on ordinary Paraguayans was perhaps even wider reaching. The media freeze saw 300 workers having their salaries suspended, initially for 90 days. About 32,000 pensioners whose public pension funds had been invested in the bank were left without payments.
“A lot of people are also not working because they can’t get paid or make payments,” said the historian and political analyst Fabián Chamorro. “Meanwhile, the protests were growing every day, and Peña’s impeachment was the way congress found to prevent a popular explosion.”
A former finance minister and ex-employee of the central bank and the International Monetary Fund, Peña was elected by promising to restore a “great Paraguay” and attract foreign investment.
Soon after taking office at age 44 as the youngest president in Paraguay’s democratic history, he appointed Carlos Carvallo Spalding, who had until then been Ueno’s CEO, to lead the central bank. Less than three months later, Spalding authorised Ueno, then a finance company, to become a digital bank.
Peña himself had about $1m in shares he bought in 2019 in a company that would become Ueno Holding in 2022, the parent company of the conglomerate that controlled Ueno Bank. Even after becoming president, he only disposed of the shares in April 2025. He said he had bought them purely as an “investor”.
“During Peña’s administration, Ueno began receiving various benefits, and the government relaxed the rules to allow public funds to be invested in the bank,” said Chamorro. An estimated $800m to $860m in state and pension funds were invested in Ueno.
A series of internal central bank reports pointing to irregularities – including loans to companies within the same group – were revealed by local media in recent months, but Peña dismissed them as a “false media campaign” against his government.
With the bank having less than half the solvency required to meet its obligations, the central bank ordered it into resolution only after mounting pressure from other banks and opposition lawmakers.
Spalding resigned and, like Peña, was ordered arrested on Friday night. During the week, police had already arrested eight senior executives and directors of Ueno and its controlling group on suspicion of concealing the bank’s deteriorating financial position for months.
The public prosecutor’s office is investigating Peña on suspicion of illicit enrichment, money laundering and influence peddling. He denies all the allegations, and his lawyers said there is no evidence he directed the allocation of pension funds to the bank.
Meanwhile, most affected people still have no access to their own money.
A guarantee fund covers deposits of up to $38,000, which would apply to more than 90% of individual account holders. On Friday, the central bank began making payments to customers with up to $1,565, no outstanding debts and an existing account at another institution.
Paola Benítez, a 25-year-old chef from the capital, Asunción, met all three requirements, but by late Friday afternoon had not yet recovered the money she had been saving for her wedding.
“This has made me a bit anxious, a bit desperate too, because honestly, who am I supposed to go to and ask about this? It’s very strange, very confusing, very sad,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Thieves walked right past it. Turns out it was the real treasure
articles.title_zh: Thieves walked right past it. Turns out it was the real treasure
articles.content_orig:
Look around your house. Could something ordinary be hiding a big secret? For one Romanian family, the answer was yes.
For decades, an elderly woman used a heavy reddish stone to hold her door open. She had picked it up from a stream near Colți, a village in southeast Romania, People reported. The stone was actually a 7.7-pound chunk of amber worth about $1.1 million.
Amber is tree sap's tougher cousin. It's hardened tree resin that turned into a fossil over a very long time, National Geographic explains. Trees make resin to seal up cuts in their bark.
Lockheed Martin agrees to pay $29.5 million after federal probe into DEI practices
Florida just approved a major property tax break, but new residents face a catch
Teen seriously hurt after something was thrown into a Halloween bonfire in Arizona
2 deputies killed after responding to Washington home. Here's what happened
Many babies thought to have peanut allergies may not have them, study finds
Thieves once broke into the woman's home. They took gold jewelry but left the heavy rock behind, the science site Futura reported.
After she died in 1991, a relative who inherited the house took a closer look. He sold the stone to the Romanian government. Experts in Poland found it is between 38 million and 70 million years old, ScienceAlert reported. That means it may have formed while dinosaurs still roamed Earth.
The amber is now a national treasure on display at the Buzău County Museum, where it has been since 2022. Its director told the Spanish newspaper El País it is one of the largest pieces of amber in the world.
This kind of amber, called rumanite, is found only in Romania, according to The Times of India . Its deep red, brown and nearly black colors set it apart from the lighter amber found near the Baltic Sea.

articles.title_orig: Schools scramble after Google gives AI ultimatum
articles.title_zh: Schools scramble after Google gives AI ultimatum
articles.content_orig:
Google is rightfully facing blowback for forcing K-12 schools to enable AI if they wanted to keep using Google search. The company quickly backtracked and decoupled and turned off the services by default, but made it clear search will continue to be just another AI chatbot. This mandate forces an ultimatum on educators: accept generative AI or de-google your school.
Students, teachers, and parents across the U.S. are now years into an argument about how schools should respond to the growth of AI-enabled tools. Google decided to skip this debate and take this choice from schools. In August it activated AI chatbot Gemini for 150 million K-12 students on Google Classroom, leaving educators scrambling to respond . A few months later, Google introduced a new way to turn it off — but now administrators would also be turning off Google search .
Google walked this back somewhat, clarifying that Gemini, Gemini notebook, and Search will have their own controls and will be off by default. But because of Google’s broader approach to force AI on all search users, this change is still an example of a tech monopolist pushing unwanted changes into the classroom.
It’s no secret that the biggest companies in AI  are operating at a huge loss , in the hope they can follow Uber’s enshittification playbook . Offer a cheap convenience at a major loss until old systems atrophy, then flip the script to reduce wages and raise consumer costs—whether that’s paying with cash or with data.
This puts Google in the odd position of an incumbent, with around 90% of search traffic . It needs to not only make good on its own AI investment, but protect its dominance from new AI tools. It’s not just enough to offer its own AI mode, it needs to turn search into AI mode, while engaging in clumsy self-preferencing that is eating its own ad revenue .
The problem with this approach is the public is split on AI, to put it mildly. Some users will welcome these changes, but the rest are stuck in an all-or-nothing bargain. Anyone concerned about the accuracy of AI overviews or their impact on click-through rates for online communities and small publishers can just deal with it . The bet is any inconvenience in switching to an alternative is enough to keep you trapped.
Google can and should offer a way to disable AI overviews. Smaller services like DuckDuckGo* and Brave search have simple and persisting AI settings which don’t require login. These services also don't mince words and make a distinction between generated AI summaries, suspected AI results, and the backend use of AI to curate links.
It’s not enough to point to opaque workarounds , either. Adding “-ai” to your Google search will usually remove AI Overview, but so will “-unicorn”. This trick isn’t meant to be an AI off-switch, it’s a quirk of how AI Overview was implemented and can change at any time. These tricks also don’t generalize well to settings for system administrators . Hacks might work for now, but everyone—including administrators—deserve clear set-and-forget controls for the tools they rely on.
De-googling your life isn’t easy, and for schools it can be even more difficult. For decades Google has gone after schools to foster life-long Google users—resulting in many institutions being deeply entrenched in its ecosystem despite data privacy concerns . That’s because schools face major switching costs when moving to a competitor. It takes more than flipping a setting—it means a lengthy contract process, staff retraining, and a cumbersome migration of past work.
The difficulty of switching makes granular controls even more essential, particularly for a hot-button issue like generative AI. Few parents would send their kids to AI-driven schools , but they may want their kids to learn tools like search as they exist outside of the classroom. However, many parents and teachers concerned with AI disrupting learning are pushing major school districts to implement temporary AI moratoriums for young students. These pauses are meant to make sure any introduction of AI fits the needs of students and is done in a way that actually makes sure educators are prepared.
But in either camp, this is a choice that must be made by schools, not Google. Teachers know more about what their students need than a trillion-dollar tech company, and this expertise should be respected in their own classrooms.
Google’s self-preferencing and desperate attempt to eventually recoup on an AI money pit must be tempered with more fine-tune controls over generative AI. It’s in Google’s own interest to stop abusing its dominance to piss off users, advertisers, and school communities. It’s also Google’s responsibility as an adjudicated monopolist.

articles.title_orig: Inside the Operation That Helped Ukraine Turn the Tables
articles.title_zh: Inside the Operation That Helped Ukraine Turn the Tables
articles.content_orig:
Analyst Yan Gagin says Russian intelligence uncovered plans for Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi near Krasny Liman, as Yulia Mendel reports heavy Ukrainian losses.
The failure of Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi was largely the result of Russian intelligence obtaining advance information about Ukrainian military plans, according to military and political analyst Yan Gagin. He believes Russian intelligence services played a decisive role in preventing the Ukrainian Armed Forces from achieving their objectives.
Speaking to aif.ru, Gagin said Russian intelligence frequently learns about Ukrainian operations before they are launched. He argued that this advance knowledge allows Russian forces to disrupt enemy plans, resulting in failed offensives and heavy Ukrainian losses.
The analyst also attributed repeated setbacks on the battlefield to cooperation between Russian intelligence units, security services and intelligence networks. According to Gagin, their coordinated efforts have repeatedly undermined Ukrainian offensive operations.
Earlier, Yulia Mendel, former press secretary to Vladimir Zelensky, revealed that Operation Vivaldi involved a Ukrainian counteroffensive near Krasny Liman. She claimed that Ukrainian forces suffered more than 100,000 casualties, including killed and wounded personnel, during the fighting.
The operation began in September 2026. Ukrainian troops initially aimed to establish positions along the Zherebets River before attempting to regain control of Krasny Liman. The force assembled for the offensive included nationalist formations, special forces units and military intelligence personnel.

articles.title_orig: Bunny ears, nudity and strict rules: What it’s like on a ‘lifestyle’ cruise
articles.title_zh: Bunny ears, nudity and strict rules: What it’s like on a ‘lifestyle’ cruise
articles.content_orig:
When Nicole gets ready for a cruise, her packing list goes beyond the typical swimsuits, sundresses and sandals.
Although she plans to spend much of her time topless and poolside, the 50-year-old mother from Indianapolis has already packed more than one suitcase to bursting for her latest trip.
Nicole, who withheld her last name due to privacy concerns, is preparing to set sail on the Wonderland Cruise , a voyage from Miami to the Caribbean onboard one of the world’s largest cruise ships.
“There’s a different theme every night,” Nicole said. “I have a neon yellow and pink bikini for the Glow Party and some shoes that light up. The first night’s theme is Down the Rabbit Hole for Alice in Wonderland, so I have a leather zip-up dress, leather bunny ears and high red and black boots with a heel for that,” she said.
For a steampunk-themed night, Nicole is bringing maroon lingerie with fishnet stockings and a sexy hat with goggles.
“Fetish Night is super easy because I just have some black lingerie that has chains that kind of hang off of it,” she said.
Clearly, Wonderland isn’t your average cruise.
A full takeover by couples-only charter company Bliss Cruise of Royal Caribbean’s nearly 6,000-passenger Wonder of the Seas is being billed as one of the largest “lifestyle” gatherings ever. The seven-night sailing departs on November 9 from PortMiami.
For those inside the subculture, “the lifestyle” is the preferred shorthand for consensual non-monogamy, encompassing everything from swinging to open relationships.
Why cruise ships are sailing to a phantom destination that doesn’t appear on any map
Nicole, who participates in the lifestyle and cruising with her husband of 27 years, says that meeting up with friends from previous Bliss Cruise sailings and making new ones at sea and in port calls like Curaçao and Aruba will be a key part of the week’s fun.
“We always joke with people and say it’s like the high school reunion that you want to go to,” she said.
For some, lifestyle cruises answer a call of the wild and offer the chance to let loose at sea beyond the usual casino tables, ice skating spectacles, waterslides and snorkeling excursions.
It’s a tourism sector that appears to be growing. While cruise industry organization Cruise Lines International Association did not respond to CNN Travel’s questions about this charter-cruise niche, “lifestyle” cruisers have noted more options on larger ships.
“What we’re seeing today is a not just a growth in the number of (lifestyle cruise) brands, but a significant increase in the size of the boats they occupy,” said Mickey Gordon, who hosts the podcast Casual Swinger . Gordon, who also uses a pseudonym for privacy reasons, said that while lifestyle cruises used to be niche events with 800 or so travelers, today’s ships are some of the largest at sea, easily selling out with 5,000 guests or more at a time.
And the reason these cruises are so popular is simple, Gordon said.
“There is simply nowhere on earth you can go that has more ‘people like me’ than a lifestyle cruise. That fact alone sells the trip,” he said.
The Wonderland Cruise, which has been sold out since March 2026 , says it will welcome 5,802 registered guests, all 21 and older, onboard Wonder of the Seas.
They hail predominantly from the United States, which accounts for 87% of bookings, followed by Canada and other nations. Bliss Cruise said guests from 47 countries will be aboard.
Passengers on the cruise represent a near-even split between male and female guests. It’s a requirement that each cabin has at least one man and one woman. “Throuples,” in this case three people with at least one man and woman among them, are permitted to share a cabin (foursomes with two women and two men, while rare, are also allowed). Just over half of passengers on the Wonderland Cruise are between the ages of 45 and 59, according to the company.
Super-sized cruise ships are becoming the norm. Is there an end in sight?
Cabin rates for bookings made in December 2024 ranged between $1,630 per person for interior cabins and more than $21,000 per person for the Royal Loft Suite.
“We do a full charter of the entire ship. We essentially buy the cruise from the cruise line, and then we market that as a specialized lifestyle cruise charter,” Russell Stephens, the CEO of Bliss Cruise, told CNN Travel.
Despite popular misconceptions about lifestyle events, he said the goal isn’t an uninhibited free-for-all, but rather creating a secure, judgment-free space for open-minded couples.
“I think people can expect a lot of fun, and it’s not what some people would perhaps expect,” said Stephens, who said he is in “the lifestyle.”
“It’s really about providing a sex-positive experience for open-minded people,” he said.
Like many major cruises, Bliss has its own app that registered passengers can access before their vacation to browse the hour-by-hour activities offered each day of the cruise, communicate with other guests who have RSVPed for the same events and create personal pages similar to dating profiles.
Categories like “life Interests” — with options as benign as boating, cars, reading, cooking and parenting — are followed by “sex interests,” including dirty talk, massage and hot wife (“a married or partnered woman who engages in consensual sexual relationships with other people — typically men — with the full knowledge, consent, and often encouragement of her primary partner”), among others that are far more risqué.
The cruise’s app details workshops and seminars, many of which cost an additional fee and are already sold out. These range from relatively tame breathwork courses and speed dating sessions to kink and fetish workshops.
There are multiple daily meet-and-greets at bars and other ship venues, too, for people who fall into categories such as Under 45, Over 45, French, Veterans, Sober & Sexy, Silver & Sexy (seniors) and Hall Pass, which is described in the app as not a pass “to have sex in the hallways,” but rather “permission from your partner to engage in sexual activity without your partner being present.”
Meeting and talks geared toward newbies are also plentiful.
“There are a lot of workshops around just being new to the lifestyle and what that is,” Stephens said. “So we try to cater for people, and we really try to welcome newbies into the lifestyle. It’s sort of like they want to think about it, they’re dipping their toes into it, they’ve kind of had a fantasy or whatever. But maybe they’ve never done anything.
“We don’t want people like deer in the headlights,” when they come onboard, he said.
Bliss Cruise is not the only operator catering to lifestyle voyagers.
Other major players include Desire Cruises , a couples-only option with sailings in the Caribbean, the Mediterranean and Adriatic Seas, Asia and North Africa. LLV Club sells lifestyle cruise itineraries in places like Fiji and Tahiti along with South Korea and Japan. Killing Kittens also offers options on the high seas.
On land, there are hotels aimed at the lifestyle-curious and veterans alike, such as Hedonism II in Jamaica, where the mantra is “Be Wicked for a Week.”
‘The Love Boat’: How a TV show transformed the cruise industry
Lifestyle vacations attract a wide cross-section of society, Stephens said. Desire passengers who were interviewed by CNN Travel agreed.
“We’ve met CEOs, we’ve met housewives, we’ve met people in real estate, people who work for the National Security Agency, lots of lawyers and doctors, hotel owners, a math teacher and crazy rich Asians,” said Alice, a physician from the New York City area who has been on two Desire cruises with her husband Bob, a doctor. (The couple spoke under pseudonyms to protect their privacy.)

articles.title_orig: Trump’s midterm drubbing adds to the populist right’s losses. France’s Le Pen could still win
articles.title_zh: Trump’s midterm drubbing adds to the populist right’s losses. France’s Le Pen could still win
articles.content_orig:
European far-right leaders quick to distance themselves from US president and stress their own priorities
Europe live – latest updates
US midterms live – latest updates
The historic Republican defeat in the US midterm elections has forcibly reminded Europe’s far-right leaders of their perennial Donald Trump dilemma: they may love his nativist agenda, but the man himself is a toxic electoral liability.
Since his re-election in 2024, European populist leaders such as Marine Le Pen in France and Giorgia Meloni in Italy have carefully calibrated their public postures towards the US president, walking a delicate transatlantic tightrope.
They adore his policies on hard borders, culture wars and anti-globalism. But European voters, even on the far right , detest Trump’s personal volatility, geopolitical unpredictability, unreliability on Europe’s defence, and trade protectionism.
Trump’s territorial threats over Greenland and economic nationalism have proved particular problems: no leader who champions national sovereignty and domestic jobs could back threats to invade the largely self-governing territory of an EU member state or punitive trade tariffs.
The sheer scale of Tuesday’s Republican wipeout has now prompted Europe’s populists to distance themselves yet further while taking away one big lesson: angry, economically squeezed voters topple incumbents.
Across European capitals on Wednesday, far-right politicians were actively insulating themselves from the White House, while dutifully avoiding any personal attacks.
Jordan Bardella, the leader of the National Rally (RN) in France and a possible prime minister if Le Pen wins next year’s presidential ballot, led the charge. Without naming the president who ordered them, Bardella blamed the US attacks on Iran, which he said had carried “very heavy consequences” for world economies.
In Germany, Alice Weidel, a co-leader of Alternative für Deutschland, said Trump had promised his voters “not to pursue an interventionist foreign policy” and that “this broken campaign promise has now come back to haunt the Republicans”.
In Italy , Roberto Vannacci, the founder of the insurgent far-right National Future party, also said the result showed the political dangers of failing to deliver on electoral promises. “Trump failed to live up to expectations,” he said.
In Madrid, the Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, dumped all pretence of a Washington connection, brushing off questions about an ideological alliance by saying he was “in Spain , not in Michigan” and cared “quite little about what happens in other places”.
Mujtaba Rahman, of the Eurasia Group consultancy, said all were acting for domestic advantage, hoping still to benefit from the “ideological momentum of Trumpism” without being tarred by the “chaos and economic disruption of his presidency”.
For far-right parties in opposition, however, the US midterms offer a clear playbook: mounting public anger over rising prices and unaffordable housing can be channelled into electoral victory. That is clearly the hope of the National Rally in France .
Bardella has repeatedly said purchasing power and the cost of living would be “the absolute priority” of an RN government, with plans to cut VAT on electricity, gas and fuel and allow employers to boost wages without additional payroll charges.
In Spain, Vox is similarly weaponising soaring living costs and plunging housing affordability against the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, in hopes of entering government as partner in a rightwing coalition after elections on 29 November.
after newsletter promotion
For populist leaders already in power in Europe, such as Meloni, that is not good news. The Italian prime minister has already faced several waves of domestic protest in Rome, Milan and elsewhere, some of them violent, over fuel costs and inflation.
Her coalition partner Matteo Salvini, leader of the far-right League, conceded that the US vote was “influenced above all by the wars, international tensions and the increase in the cost of living, the consequences of which fall directly on families”.
Opposition MPs were equally quick to connect the dots, noting that Trump had pledged to lower prices and bring back quality jobs, but that never happened. And once in power, far-right leaders who fail to deliver are as vulnerable to voter anger as any others.
Some on the European far right, such Dan Dungaciu of Romania’s AUR, sought to play down Trump’s crushing defeat by arguing that reports of his “political death” were greatly exaggerated, but the broader political lesson may go beyond the populists.
The electoral fortunes of Europe’s far right, whose nationalist leaders will in all probability continue espousing Maga’s ideas while keeping Trump himself at arm’s length, do not depend on the success or failure of the US president at the ballot box.
The underlying grievances driving the rise of European populism – the cost of living, the housing crises, the rural-urban divide, arguments about immigration – are rooted firmly in European domestic conditions, not in American election results.
Some warn the worst consequence of these midterms would be for Europe’s mainstream parties to assume they showed the populist tide was receding. What they actually showed was that voter anger over the cost of living is unforgiving – whoever is in power.

articles.title_orig: This Israeli Vows to Oust Netanyahu. Here’s How.
articles.title_zh: This Israeli Vows to Oust Netanyahu. Here’s How.
articles.content_orig:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog must decide who gets the first attempt at forming a government, after an inconclusive election left both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, short of a parliamentary majority.
Herzog has said he will task a candidate with forming a government on Sunday. Eisenkot has received the endorsement of a majority of lawmakers – but only thanks to parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, which won a record 19 seats in October’s election, but whom Eisenkot has ruled out bringing into government.
During consultations between party heads and Herzog , which ended on Thursday, 67 out of 120 Knesset members endorsed Eisenkot, while only 46 endorsed Netanyahu.
Netanyahu’s endorsements fell seven short of his bloc’s 53 seats after United Torah Judaism, one of his longtime allies, withheld endorsements over his coalition’s failure to exempt ultra-Orthodox Israelis from military service.
Herzog has not publicly committed to either side, saying that while the numbers may look clear, “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” made it hard to tell who could build a coalition.
Prior to the October 27 elections, reports emerged that the president wanted to push for a national unity government between Netanyahu and Eisenkot’s rival parties to avoid another election.
No bloc has secured the 61 seats needed to form a majority government. Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious alliance has 53, four Jewish-led parties backing Eisenkot hold 48, and the Arab-led parties hold 19.
Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties, which would give him a 67-seat bloc. Winning over the two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats.
United Torah Judaism has signalled that its support was available for the right price, but Shas endorsed Netanyahu on Wednesday.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, would need to lure an opposition party to his side. A unity government with the two men rotating as prime minister – and excluding Arab-led parties from government – is another option, but many Netanyahu rivals have ruled out serving under him.
So far, it seems unlikely that they will.
The Arab-led parties are the Joint List, an alliance of three parties, and the United Arab List (Ra’am). They hold 11 and eight seats, respectively.
Ra’am says it is willing to join an Eisenkot-led government, while the Joint List has ruled out joining but offered to help put him in office from the outside.
Both endorsed Eisenkot during consultations with President Herzog, but he has refused to bring either into government unless they meet certain conditions, including recognising Hamas as a “terrorist organisation”.
Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas, whose party joined an anti-Netanyahu coalition in 2021 and became the first party representing Palestinians to enter government in Israel, has expressed support for disarming Hamas, but declined to label it as a “terror” group.
However, Israeli law allows Eisenkot to become prime minister with fewer than 61 seats if his proposed government wins a parliamentary confidence vote – which the two could help him secure.
Eisenkot could form a minority government in the meantime and later secure a majority by luring the two ultra-Orthodox parties by making concessions on the conscription issue.
In positions that many observers see as highlighting the second-class nature of Palestinian citizens in Israel, some of Eisenkot’s allies have opposed any reliance on Palestinian lawmakers, while Netanyahu’s Likud has threatened that cooperating with the Arab-led parties would be “dangerous to Israel”.
Senior Joint List member Ahmad Tibi told The Associated Press that rejecting a partnership would prove Israel is “an ethnocracy, not an absolute democracy for all citizens”.
First, an end to Netanyahu’s rule.
The Joint List said its unanimous backing for Eisenkot answered a “public demand” to stop Netanyahu and his government returning to power.
By widening Eisenkot’s lead, it said, it hoped to narrow the path to a unity government that keeps Netanyahu in office. Its support, it added, did not mean dropping its reservations about an opposition that had not shown readiness to confront Netanyahu’s approach or incitement against Palestinian citizens of Israel.
In return for outside support, Arab-led parties are seeking guarantees for Palestinian citizens, including an end to house demolitions and incitement, action against crime, and a political horizon for Palestinians.
Tibi told The AP he had no illusions that this would end Israel’s wars or bring a Palestinian state, but said a “repair government” would improve Palestinian citizens’ lives, including, potentially, by tackling violent crime in their communities.
Ra’am leader Abbas has also said ending the government of Netanyahu, and far-right figures such as Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, is a priority.
The nominee chosen by Herzog will have 28 days to form a coalition, extendable by 14 more. If they fail, another nominee will be chosen and granted 28 days.
If the second nominee fails, a parliament majority can back a third candidate, and be granted a final 14 days.
If once again no government is formed, the Knesset will be dissolved and an entirely new election called within 90 days. This would mean Netanyahu staying on as caretaker prime minister.
Nehru Jamhour, an analyst of Israeli affairs, told Al Jazeera that this drawn-out impasse was the likeliest outcome, and Netanyahu’s preferred one. He said that Netanyahu was hoping that a repeat election could weaken his rivals and depress turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
