articles.title_orig: Top Gulf official offers glimmer of hope on Trump-Iran nuclear talks as threat of war hangs over region
articles.title_zh: Top Gulf official offers glimmer of hope on Trump-Iran nuclear talks as threat of war hangs over region
articles.content_orig:
Reporting from Dubai, Fox News Digital examines how the UAE is balancing hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough with preparations for escalation, as Emirati officials and experts warn of Iran's threats to regional security and the global economy.
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — A senior United Arab Emirates official says he is cautiously optimistic about negotiations between the United States and Iran, citing progress through Qatari mediation over the past days, even as fears of renewed military confrontation continue to grip the Middle East .
"We see some progress. … We hope that both sides will be able to reach a point where they will start building trust and engaging in a way to avoid the war, to find a political solution. … I am a little bit optimistic, but I don't exclude the other option," Dr. Ali Rashid Al Nuaimi, chairman of the Defense, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee of the UAE's Federal National Council, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.
His remarks came as Reuters reported on Nov. 5 that Iran had submitted a new nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar. Tehran, however, continued to insist that the U.S. meet seven conditions before negotiations could proceed, including sanctions relief and an end to the American naval blockade.
IS THIS TRUMP’S LAST ‘LAST CHANCE’? CEASELESS STRING OF BROKEN CEASEFIRES FUELS DOUBT OVER IRAN DEAL
Dr. Ali Rashid Al Nuaimi, chairman of the UAE Federal National Council's Defense, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee, speaks to Fox News Digital in Abu Dhabi about the Iranian threat, regional security and prospects for diplomacy. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
President Donald Trump has not ruled out further military operations, while Iran has threatened broader retaliation if fighting resumes.
For the UAE, which endured thousands of Iranian missile and drone attacks earlier this year, the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough offers hope. But its leaders are making clear that hope cannot replace preparedness.
"We plan for the worst. We hope for the best. … We always make sure that we are ready to deal with all the challenges or the threats," Al Nuaimi said.
That combination of optimism and caution was evident during Fox News Digital's reporting trip across the Emirates, where daily life appeared remarkably normal despite the uncertainty surrounding the country.
On an evening in downtown Dubai, restaurant terraces were packed, tourists filled the streets and crowds gathered around a fountain show set to music that moved between Arabic songs and Western pop hits.
Businesses were operating, international visitors were arriving and the city continued to project an image of prosperity and openness.
IRAN’S STRAIT OF HORMUZ SCHEME COULD DERAIL ONE GULF NATION’S BRIGHT FUTURE
Crowds gather to enjoy an evening fountain show in downtown Dubai, United Arab Emirates, as daily life continues despite the threat of renewed regional conflict with Iran. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
The contrast was just as striking in Abu Dhabi, where Fox News Digital attended the opening of ADIPEC 2026 , one of the world's largest energy conferences, against the backdrop of continuing tensions with Iran and the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz.
Days before the conference, ExxonMobil and Chevron executives had canceled their planned appearances because of security concerns, Reuters reported on Oct. 29.
Yet inside the exhibition halls, delegates from around the world gathered to discuss investment, announce partnerships and explore technological solutions to the energy crisis .
It was a demonstration of the UAE's determination to keep its economy moving while preparing for a security environment that has changed dramatically.
TRUMP ADMIN THREATENS IRAN WITH 'CONSEQUENCES' AS ALLIES CONVENE AMID THREATS OF POST-ELECTION ESCALATION
United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan greets President Donald Trump at Abu Dhabi International Airport on Thursday, May 15, 2025. (AP Photo/Altaf Qadri)
The UAE has already paid a significant price for its proximity to the conflict.
More than 3,000 Iranian missiles and drones targeted the Emirates during the war, according to figures cited by The Associated Press on Nov. 2. The attacks caused casualties and damage to civilian infrastructure.Although no new Iranian attacks had targeted the UAE since May, the threat of renewed confrontation has kept the country on alert.
Al Nuaimi emphasized that while the UAE considers itself a nation committed to peace, it will not hesitate to protect its population.
"Every nation, when it is attacked, [has] the right to defend their people, their sovereignty, their nation," he said.
But he also drew a clear distinction between the Iranian regime and the Iranian people, who are repressed by the regime. "The Iranian people deserve to be respected, accepted. They have great values, great civilization, and they are our neighbor."
MIDDLE EAST TAKES CENTER STAGE AT UN AS REGIONAL LEADERS CONFRONT IRAN WAR, GAZA AND HOUTHI THREAT
A man walks past a housing compound as a tall plume of black smoke ascends following an explosion in the Fujairah industrial zone on March 3, 2026. Iran's strikes on Gulf neighbours since February 28, following the US-Israeli attack, forced the UAE to shut its airspace, blindsiding travellers who thought they were headed to one of the region's safest holiday destinations. (Fadel SENNA / AFP via Getty Images)
Despite the confrontation with Iran, Al Nuaimi rejected the suggestion that the UAE's relationship with Washington should be judged primarily through the current conflict or any particular U.S. administration.
"We don't see our relationship with the United States through these conflicts, through security and defense. No, it's a partnership. It's a strategic partnership. It is a sustainable partnership. … Our main partnership is with the United States as a nation, with the American people."
He emphasized that the relationship extends across education, medicine, technology, energy and investment, and is intended to endure political changes in Washington.
"We don't look at the United States through a certain administration. Our engagement and partnership with the United States ... [is] with the nation. It's with the people. ... We have the flexibility and the ability to [adapt] and engage with any administration."
The comments come at a sensitive time for Gulf governments, whose security relationships with Washington have become more consequential as Iran threatens regional infrastructure and international shipping.
At ADIPEC's opening ceremony on Nov. 2, Dr. Sultan Al Jaber, the UAE's minister of industry and advanced technology and chief executive of state-owned energy giant ADNOC, emphasized that the country's ability to withstand the crisis was the result of years of preparation. "We did not write our resilience playbook during this disruption. We wrote it years before," Al Jaber told the audience.
The message was consistent with what officials and analysts repeatedly emphasized during Fox News Digital's visit: the UAE intends to remain a reliable international partner despite the possibility of another regional escalation.
GULF COUNTRIES STRONGLY CONDEMN IRAN'S DRONE ATTACK ON BAHRAIN AS RISING TENSIONS THREATEN MOU
The exhibition floor at ADIPEC 2026 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, where global energy companies showcased new technologies and innovations amid growing concerns over energy security and regional instability. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
In a separate exclusive interview with Fox News Digital in Dubai, Mohammed Baharoon, director general of the Emirati research center B'huth, argued that the confrontation with Iran has fundamentally expanded the meaning of national security.
"Our resilience now becomes our deterrence," Baharoon said.
The UAE's security strategy, he explained, involves far more than intercepting missiles and drones. It also means ensuring reliable energy supplie

articles.title_orig: Hackers probed Europe’s fridge systems weeks before cyberattacks. Who did it and what could they target next?
articles.title_zh: Hackers probed Europe’s fridge systems weeks before cyberattacks. Who did it and what could they target next?
articles.content_orig:
Cybersecurity researchers say they detected hackers probing internet-connected refrigeration systems across Europe in the days before a wave of cyberattacks and incidents disrupted supermarkets and blood banks, with evidence suggesting it may have been part of a coordinated operation.
Refrigeration systems in supermarkets across nine European countries as well as several blood banks in France were attacked on 2 and 3 November.
Hackers exploited weak cybersecurity and vulnerabilities in manufacturer Danfoss’s AK-SM refrigeration system manager to put fridges and freezers on defrost settings, in some cases temperatures were set as high 50 degrees Celsius.
The incidents forced many grocery stores to throw away spoiled produce from their fridges and freezers and have become a very visible example of how easily cyberattacks can disrupt everyday life by targeting infrastructure systems that are often taken for granted.
For cybersecurity firm Lupovis, the signs point to a coordinated operation potentially involving a state actor — one that was preceded by days of probing.
The company says it saw a period of reconnaissance targeting these systems just days before the attacks.
The company observed over 276 attempts coming from 91 different threat actors matching specific components of Danfoss controllers during this 10-day period. Activity peaking on 26 October, before coming to a halt at the end of the month.
“Between the 20th and 30th of October, what we saw was a wave of what we call reconnaissance,” CEO Xavier Bellekens told Euronews Next.
“We see a huge peak suddenly for 10 days where adversaries are trying the default passwords. They are trying a couple of those vulnerabilities.”
Lupovis operates a system of so-called “honeypots”, which replicate its clients’ online systems and technologies. The company equips them with sensors and then deliberately exposes them to hackers, encouraging attacks so it can track how these systems are accessed and exploited.
This intelligence can then be used to identify vulnerabilities without putting the clients' real systems at risk.
It was through this system that Lupovis, whose clients include the Scottish government, Orange, Telefonica and a number of retail companies, detected what it describes as “reconnaissance” on Danfoss systems in the days before November’s attacks.
“You can think of it as like burglars, driving through your neighbourhood and identifying the houses they are going to go and break into,” said Bellekens.
Lupovis then traced what it describes as the digital "breadcrumbs" left by the probing and attacks, finding that so-called "bulletproof hosting" was used — web hosting services that are designed to resist takedown requests and law enforcement intervention.
“On the one hand, you have Amazon Web Services, they are the opposite of a bullet-proof hosting. If you do something malicious with one of their servers, that's it, they cancel your account. Bulletproof hosting is the opposite. You do something malicious, It's out of jurisdiction," Bellekens said.
Lupovis then examined the hosting providers themselves.
“We realised that some of those bulletproof hosting had been used by Russian groups in the past,” says Bellekens.
The company is clear that just because servers are located somewhere does not necessarily mean that the people using it share the same nationality, so they cannot say for sure that Russia is behind the attacks.
“However, there's a bit of a pattern here,” says the Lupovis CEO, “So we are looking for someone that has the capability to attack certain countries in particular.”
According to the CEO, Lupovis sensors in South America, Africa, North America and Asia did not record the same activity. It was only picked up by sensors in Europe.
He also believes the ability to coordinate attacks across Europe helps narrow down the list of suspects.
“You [the attacker] have to be able to coordinate this attack because most of it happened within a 24-hour period.”
“All of this makes us point to an adversary that, to us, is not a script kiddie [an unskilled amateur]. They are not a lone wolf. It looks like a well-planned operation. So a state fits the bill.”
“When we pull on the thread it does look like it could well be Russia. So, that is basically where we're at.”
The incidents come amid wider concerns about hybrid threats and suspected Russian-linked activity targeting European countries.
However, the precise identity and motivation of the attackers remain unclear.
George Nott, technology editor at The Grocer, said the attacks appeared to have relied on relatively basic security weaknesses rather than highly advanced hacking techniques.
"Attackers managed to access refrigeration systems by simply finding their log-in pages on the open internet, and exploiting already patched vulnerabilities and weak passwords rather than some highly advanced technology," he told Euronews Next.
Nott also cautioned against drawing firm conclusions about who was responsible.
"it's still unclear who was behind the attack or what they hoped to achieve. We'll have to face the fact we may never known. With no ransom demand or claim of responsibility, it could have been anyone from a state-sponsored actor to a gang of teenagers 'doing it for the lols'."
Cybersecurity agencies in the countries affected this week have differed in how they describe the incidents. Belgium, Luxembourg, Italy, Portugal and Estonia have called them a “cyberattack”, while Sweden and Ireland referred to it as a “cyber incident”.
The European Union’s Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) has also stopped short of explicitly calling the incidents a cyberattack.
Hackers were able to access refrigeration systems across Europe because controller boxes connected to the internet were being used to remotely manage refrigeration units, Bellekens said.
Remote control of such devices is common in today’s increasingly digital world. However, the Lupovis CEO says many of the systems could have been better protected had they been placed on virtual private networks (VPNs) rather than exposed directly to the internet.
“[It] would have entirely mitigated the risk because like a VPN is more complex to exploit," he said.
To make matters worse, many of the systems were reportedly accessible using factory-default credentials, such as "Username" Supervisor" and "Password: 12345", suggesting that basic security measures had not been implemented.
Nott said the problem reflets a wider tendency in the retail sector to overlook the security of connected equipment.
“The security of connected equipment across the retail sector can overlooked — the priority given to more obvious targets such as payment systems and customer data," he said.
Once hackers had gained access to the refrigeration control systems they were able to switch them to defrost mode and ramp up the temperatures, spoiling goods stored in fridges and freezers across Europe.
The attacks have raised concerns about the security of other internet-connected equipment, from supermarket machinery to the systems that control access, heating and ventilation in buildings.
Nott warned the future attacks may not be confined to refrigeration systems.
"more and more of the systems that keep supermarkets running — heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems; electronic shelf labels; floor cleaning robots — could all present similar vulnerabilities if remote access isn't properly secured and software patched," he said.
But the potential exposure goes well beyond retail.
"The freezer is not special. It is just the most visible example of a much bigger category,” says Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security, a global provider of integrated physical security.
“The same kind of small, internet-connected controller that was used to warm up those fridges also runs the doors, the access-control readers, the cameras, the alarms, the lighting and the heating and ventilation in most modern buildings.”

articles.title_orig: How Democrats used anger over data centers to flip red states
articles.title_zh: How Democrats used anger over data centers to flip red states
articles.content_orig:
As the dust settled on Election Night, Democratic operatives working to elect James Talarico were surprised by the breadth of his victory across Texas’ 254 counties. But even then, one area stood out.
Kaufman County, southeast of Dallas, is the site of two massive data center projects that have sparked local backlash. The largest city in the county, Forney, is already working to outlaw new data centers within its city limits.
The solidly red county was one of 55 counties where a pro-Talarico super PAC, Lone Star Rising PAC, targeted voters within 5 miles of a proposed or approved data center project. The PAC sent them a series of mail pieces and digital ads blaming the project on the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton.
“WARNING,” one of the mailers read, addressing the voters by their first names and adding, “There is an existing or proposed data center near you in Kaufman County. Ken Paxton made it easier to build.”
Talarico carried Kaufman County by 1 percentage point as he notched a striking 12-point victory statewide, helping lead Democrats to statewide victory in Texas for the first time since 1994.
It was one of many examples where backlash to data centers fueled Democrats’ staggering victories in the midterms. From statewide races to local ballot initiatives, voters demonstrated sweeping support for a tougher stance toward data centers, if not outright opposition to their continued development.
About a quarter of voters said AI and data centers were “crucial” to their vote in the midterms, trailing higher priorities such as the cost of living and corruption, according to CNN’s Voter Poll. But when voters were asked about building data centers in their communities, they were overwhelmingly opposed by a roughly 3-to-1 margin.
“It was overwhelming, unequivocal, bipartisan backlash from the bottom up that was showing up in every corner of my district,” said Michigan Rep.-elect Will Lawrence, who flipped a Republican-held House seat after centering his campaign early on opposition to data centers.
GOP candidates had to contend with President Donald Trump’s strongly supportive stance on data centers. By the final weeks of the election, even Trump seemed to concede the AI industry had political problems when he started proposed rebranding AI as “super intelligence.”
Some Republicans are already warning they need a different strategy on the issue for 2028.
The Alliance for a Better Future, a conservative AI policy group, issued a memo the day after the election arguing that it was “impossible to ignore the strong impact Super Intelligence (SI) policy had on this election and how connected it is to economic concerns in particular.” The memo urged Republicans to “recalibrate” and “course correct” ahead of 2028.
One GOP strategist involved in the midterms said any Republicans who want to be competitive in the next presidential race “needs a better playbook.”
“The economy may have been the top issue of this election, but what people are missing is that AI and data centers drove a lot of that angst,” said one GOP strategist involved in the midterms. “AI will likely move to the top of the issue grid in 2028.”
Lawrence stood out for how early – and aggressively – he staked his campaign on data centers. His first TV ad of the primary opened with him standing in the middle of a field, warning that “tech billionaires want to turn this whole field into a massive data center that will jack up your energy bills and ruin our home values.”
There was hardly a national firestorm over data centers when Lawrence attended a Howell Township planning board meeting in October 2025 to protest a proposed data center. It was one of several such meetings he went to throughout his campaign.
But by the end of the midterms, it was hard to find a race where candidates were not arguing over the issue, racing to keep up with public opinion that cut across party lines.
Democratic candidates generally talked tough on data centers, and some, such as Lawrence, even pushed federal moratoriums on them. Republicans at times echoed calls for new restrictions but also touted their economic benefits and arguing they were necessary to stay ahead of China in the AI race.
Dan Diorio, a top official at the Data Center Coalition, a trade group, argued the industry needs to do a better job of showing Americans how data centers could address their concerns about the cost of living. He argued residents of Loudoun County, Virginia, are seeing tax relief due to the data center boom there, although Virginia politics have also been reshaped by concerns about spiking electricity costs due to data center demand.
“People need to see it and feel it,” he said.
Ohio was one of the biggest battleground states for data centers.
The winner of the Senate race, Democrat Sherrod Brown, branded GOP incumbent Jon Husted as “the face of data centers,” citing his support for data center investments as lieutenant governor. The line of attack was so potent that the National Republican Senatorial Committee issued a memo in August warning that data centers were “the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”
The NRSC did not respond to a request for comment for this story.
Husted sought to neutralize the vulnerability in September by spearheading legislation to combat rising energy costs from data centers. Senate Democrats blocked it .
The battle also played out at the local level. Voters in at least 10 Ohio cities passed charter amendments to ban construction of large data centers, according to the anti-data center group Conserve Ohio. The ballot measure in Granville, which is outside Columbus, received over 80 percent support.
In another red state — South Carolina — Democrat Annie Andrews pulled off a major upset in the Senate after persistently labeling the Republican incumbent, Darline Graham, as “Data Center Darline.” Andrews flipped Colleton County, which voted for Trump by 19 percentage points. It was one of the counties that Andrews visited to speak out against local data center developments.
The issue was a vulnerability for Graham as early as her primary, when she said during a debate that “we have to have data centers.” Her position, which she later moderated, drew attacks from multiple fellow Republicans at the time.
A new super PAC aligned with the data center industry, Building the Future, made a late push for Graham in the general election, spending $2.5 million on her behalf. But that spending fueled further attacks that she was beholden to the industry.
Data centers came up in notable ways in other House races.
Mitchell Berman, the Democrat who defeated Republican Rep. Bryan Steil of Wisconsin, ran an ad that showed him shooting a clay pigeon labeled “Data Center.” And in Arizona’s 1st Congressional District, Democrat Amish Shah prevailed after bluntly saying he did not want any data centers in his district.
Shah’s Republican opponent, Jay Feely, went for a more nuanced position, the kind that some Republicans are now second-guessing after Tuesday’s wipeout.
“We have to win [the AI race], we can’t let China win it,” Feely said in one media appearance , “but at the same time, you have to be able to talk to the person who doesn’t really care about China and this fight we’re in, who cares about their life. And so you have to make the argument about why data centers are necessary.”
In Texas, home to the second most data centers in the country, Talarico was not the only statewide winner who ran on cracking down on data centers. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa went further than Talarico did and called for a moratorium on data centers until the Legislature could pass “real protections.”
“We need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections,” Hinojosa told CNN’s Jake Tapper on Thursday. “We can have a strong economy, strong industry and protections for the people of Texas. Those things are not mutually exclusive.”

articles.title_orig: New Zealand election too close to call with 95% votes in
articles.title_zh: New Zealand election too close to call with 95% votes in
articles.content_orig:
The two main parties were effectively deadlocked in New Zealand 's close-fought general elections on Saturday, with the rising cost of living and general economic problems the main issues at stake.
Results with 95% votes counted showed the ruling center-right National Party and the opposition Labour Party neck-and-neck with just under 30% of the vote.
The National Party held a slim lead of about 3,500 votes more than Labour late on Saturday night.
Incumbent Prime Minister Cristopher Luxon, who heads the National Party, said that his party "is once again the largest party in parliament, and we have a pathway to forming the next government."
The National Party currently governs in coalition with the pro-business ACT and the right-wing populist New Zealand First. According to preliminary results, the three parties are set to net a total 67 seats in parliament, amounting to a wafer-thin majority.
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said that New Zealand's politicians would need to find "common ground" after the results showed neither his party nor the ruling National Party were likely to form a governing majority on their own.
"New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you've said," Hipkins told supporters.
"Our next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together, and to find common ground."
Special votes, including those cast from people overseas, are to be counted over the next three weeks. The votes typically benefit left-leaning parties and have shifted preliminary election results over the last three elections.
Final results are expected to be released on November 27.
If the right-wing bloc fails to hold on to its slim majority, the centrist Opportunity Party could act as a kingmaker. The party is projected to get seven seats, putting it past the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time since it was founded in 2017.
Luxon has previously ruled out cooperating with the Opportunity Party.
New Zealand has a mixed-member proportional system that requires voters to tick two options: a party and a local electoral candidate.
Electorate winners earn a seat in parliament, which typically has 120 seats, unless a so-called "overhang" leads to more lawmakers being returned to parliament, along with the highest-ranked members of the party based on their national party vote.
Preliminary results on Saturday showed that parliament is set to expand to 130 seats because of the overhang, making it the largest parliament in New Zealand history.
The vote took against a backdrop of high prices for basic goods and the highest unemployment in more than a decade.
The voting took place under New Zealand's strict laws banning media reporting and political campaigning on the final day.
New Zealanders have, however, been able to cast their votes since October 26, with almost 1.7 million of the country's 3.8 million eligible voters already casting their ballots by Thursday, according to the electoral commission.

articles.title_orig: World of Warcraft: Forever is the biggest launch in WoW history, beating Wrath itself
articles.title_zh: World of Warcraft: Forever is the biggest launch in WoW history, beating Wrath itself
articles.content_orig:
World of Warcraft: Forever launches at 3:00 p.m. PST today, and everyone’s starting from level 1. Back to the original continents, back to the long road to 60, and this time you can roll a Skyborne and start your story on Zephras Isle. Familiar roads, new surprises, and an Azeroth that keeps growing after you hit the cap. To celebrate, we’re running a week of WoW: Forever on Twitch with a new way to catch every moment, plus earn epic rewards.
The road to 60 is long, and nobody can watch every six-hour stream. So we built something for the moments you missed.
Starting this week, category pages on the Twitch website will have Stream Recaps shelves, where you can find short Recaps from recent streams pinned right above the live channels. Open the World of Warcraft category and you can catch the first Skyborne runs, the dungeon wipes and the plays everyone’s clipping, all in a few minutes.
If you’ve never watched a Recap, we’ve got you. A Recap is a short highlight reel of a stream, built from clips made by the streamer, their editors and their viewers. The new shelf brings together Recaps from streams in the World of Warcraft: Forever category, so you can catch up on streamers beyond the ones you follow. You’ll probably find a few new favorites along the way.
World of Warcraft is the first category to get Recaps, and every other category on Twitch gets them later this week. A game where every streamer starts fresh at level 1 is a pretty good place to start.
Your Stream Recap is built automatically from your stream’s clips, but you can make it your own.
With the new WoW: Forever Armory Twitch Extension, your abilities, build and equipment show up right on your channel. Viewers can see exactly how you’re playing and use it to plan their own journey through Azeroth.
Add it directly from your Creator Dashboard before your next stream.
Show your allegiance by subscribing or gifting a sub to your favorite World of Warcraft streamer to receive the Horde and Alliance chat badges!
Be sure to check out a very special stream happening right now on /warcraft . Who knows, there may be an upcoming major reveal and a particularly exciting moment you don’t want to miss!
Streamers, go live in World of Warcraft: Forever and add your Stream Recaps to get featured on the category page. And viewers, check out all the best moments from one of the biggest game launches of the year!

articles.title_orig: Six Pallets of NVIDIA Hardware Worth $11.4 Million Stolen on the Way to Texas
articles.title_zh: Six Pallets of NVIDIA Hardware Worth $11.4 Million Stolen on the Way to Texas
articles.content_orig:
OAKLAND, Calif. (KGO) -- Authorities are investigating the theft of more than $11 million worth of Nvidia computer hardware in Oakland, in what experts describe as a sophisticated cargo heist targeting one of the world's most valuable technology companies.
According to reporting by the Bay Area News Group, the theft involved $11.4 million worth of Nvidia cargo that disappeared after departing Oakland on its way to Texas.
The shipment, consisting of six pallets of Nvidia hardware, left Oakland on Aug. 29 and was bound for Fort Worth, Texas. Authorities said the cargo was picked up as planned by a truck identified as a food transport company.
Investigators later lost track of the vehicle in San Bernardino County.
In a statement, Oakland police said: "The Oakland Police Department is investigating a grand theft that occurred in East Oakland. The victim reported the crime to OPD on September 13, 2026."
Olaf Groth, a professor at UC Berkeley's Haas School of Business and has expertise in artificial intelligence, emerging technology and global economics, said Nvidia chips are highly sought after.
"There's lots and lots of incentives to hijack those chips anywhere where security is weak," Groth said.
He said the chips can command significantly higher prices outside the United States.
"These chips command about double the price that they command inside the United States. So, if a chip costs about $550,000, then they go for about 1 million or more abroad," Groth said.
The theft is the latest in a series of crimes targeting high-value technology shipments in the Bay Area. Last year, police in Fremont and Union City investigated burglaries involving Nvidia cargo valued at more than $7.5 million.
Groth said the scale and complexity of such thefts suggest increasingly sophisticated criminal operations.
"Because the cargoes are getting bigger. The heists are getting more complex and that will point toward a professionalization of the teams that are hijacking these," he said.
An ABC7 viewer also provided video of a separate attempted theft in September. According to police, suspects believed they were targeting trucks carrying expensive Nvidia technology. The trucks instead contained 40,000 pounds of sand.
Groth said the incidents highlight broader concerns about protecting advanced computing technology.
"Security has to get a lot tighter around these because they're a national security asset," he said.
He also raised concerns about where stolen hardware could ultimately end up.
"This is a national security concern as well because we don't know where these chips are going. They could be going to China, they could be anywhere where we have conflict in the world," Groth said.
Authorities have not announced any arrests in the $11.4 million theft, and the investigation remains ongoing.
Experts say the case underscores growing concerns about the security of high-value technology shipments and the potential national security implications when advanced computer hardware enters the black market.

articles.title_orig: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.title_zh: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.content_orig:
ABOARD THE PAPAL FLIGHT — Three countries in 12 days, a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and nine Masses on a trip covering around 19,000 miles. Less than a month after Pope Leo XIV underwent cancer surgery , he set off on what the Vatican called a “homecoming” tour of South America.
The 71-year-old’s long trip across the strongly Catholic region will take him to Uruguay and Argentina, as well as to Peru, where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023.
Leo considers the tour, one of the most grueling undertaken by a Catholic leader in decades, a “homecoming to places where he spent a long time and to which he feels closely connected,” Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni told journalists at a briefing Tuesday.
The Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, told pilgrims at his weekly audience in St. Peter’s Square on Wednesday that he was ⁠hoping to “strengthen the faith, renew hope” and “rekindle the fire of charity.”
Leo will hold several meetings with survivors of sexual abuse by ​Catholic clergy during the trip, the Vatican has said, without yet providing further details.
Bruni said the pope would also address a range of issues facing the continent, including environmental destruction, ⁠arms trafficking and regional political instability, bringing “a message of communion and unity.”
Leo departed from Rome’s Fiumicino Airport early ​Friday, and arrived in Uruguay on Friday afternoon for the country’s first papal visit since 1988.
After takeoff, Leo told journalists aboard the plane that he had no doubt he would embark on the trip.
“I know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place. I confess that from the first day I had no doubt,” he said. “I was convinced that this trip had to go forward and very happy to say, praise the Lord and thanks to wonderful medical assistants, I am here today, I think, in fairly good shape.”
Asked if he had any advice for other people facing cancer, Leo replied, “Not to be afraid, early detection is obviously the best way to go, regular check ups and take care of yourself.”
Leo also noted in response to a question from NBC News that “trust in God, good doctors, good surgeons, and, overall, a healthy lifestyle” had contributed to his quick recovery.
Leo, who is the first pope to vote in a U.S. election, was also asked about the importance of voting.
“I am proud to be an American and to exercise my right,” he said.
Considered the most secular country in the region, where only a fraction of people go to Mass regularly, Uruguay was the first in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use and the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion.
In October 2025, the country of just 3.5 million people became the first in the region to approve legislation for assisted dying despite strong opposition from the Catholic Church.
After Uruguay, Leo’s tour will take him to Argentina for three days, where he is expected to meet with right-wing President Javier Milei , a close ally of President Donald Trump .
It will be the first papal visit to Argentina since Pope John Paul II traveled to the country in 1987.
Leo’s immediate predecessor, Pope Francis, was born in Argentina, the first pontiff from the region, but he declined numerous invitations to return to his homeland.
The biggest crowds of the trip are likely next week during his six-day visit to Peru, where Leo is widely celebrated as a beloved national figure. He will stop off in the capital, Lima, before visiting his former diocese of Chiclayo, where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until taking up a Vatican post in 2023.
Leo, who was treated last month for lung ‌adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, will also make several high-altitude visits in the Peruvian Andes.
Doctors have ⁠said that the disease was localized and that he would not require any further treatments; Bruni said Leo had recovered enough that no additional medical measures ⁠would be necessary during his trip.
Speaking at the same briefing Tuesday, Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief, said Leo was grateful for the concern about his health and the demands the journey might make on him.
But, she said, he was “so excited” to make the trip.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested
articles.title_zh: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested
articles.content_orig:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.
Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse earlier this week of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.
He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
He is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said.
Peña's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.
The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, Asunción.
Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.
Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.
Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," Peña said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".
Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history – a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."
Analysts say Peña is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.
His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk Staked His Empire on Texas. Now State Democrats Want to Rein Him In.
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk Staked His Empire on Texas. Now State Democrats Want to Rein Him In.
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk blew $447 million to support Republican candidates in the midterm elections — and almost every single cent of it went to waste .
But if you were about to break out a tiny violin to soundtrack the sorrows of the world’s first — and first former — trillionaire, you should consider acquiring an even tinier one, because those were just the beginning of his losses.
Shares of Musk’s businesses SpaceX and Tesla immediately tanked after Democrats swept the Senate, House, and governorship races — including in Texas, Musk’s base of operations. His automaker fell 3.3 percent, and his rocket-slash-AI company plunged by a full 3.8 , wiping out what Bloomberg reported was over $120 billion.
That did a number on Musk’s personal wealth, which in large part derives from his stakes in those companies. He is now, by the Financial Time’s estimate , some $30 billion poorer.
Despite the excess of egg on his face, Musk still managed to look through his post history on X and start deleting the ones about the election.
Trying to rally his followers, Musk tweeted “Vote red today!” on Tuesday morning. But it was removed after the reality of a blue tsunami came crashing at his doorstep. So was his pinned tweet from last week urging his followers to vote for Republican senators, which according to Forbes was taken down around the time Democratic candidate James Talarico declared victory in the senate race.
To his credit, he did make a few jokes at his own expense.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he tweeted late Tuesday night.
For the most part, though, Musk seems eager to move on. Besides one post in which he claimed “Voter ID failed in California,” he’s gone back to his usual tweets promoting Grok and his various companies almost as if nothing happened. If we spent half a billion dollars trying to get candidates elect who all lost, and were now staring down the barrel of a Democrat-stacked government looking to get revenge on us , we would probably try to sweep everything under the rug, too.

articles.title_orig: China, EU urged to deepen cooperation amid global transitions
articles.title_zh: China, EU urged to deepen cooperation amid global transitions
articles.content_orig:
China and the European Union should strengthen dialogue, manage their differences and expand cooperation in emerging areas such as artificial intelligence to ensure the stable development of their relationship over the next 50 years, Chinese Ambassador to the EU Cai Run said on Thursday.
Speaking at the 14th China-Europe Forum in Brussels, Cai said the two sides should remain committed to their partnership, resolve economic and trade disputes through consultation, and respect each other's core interests and major concerns.
"We are partners, not rivals, still less adversaries," Cai said. "China is not the source of the economic problems facing the EU, but a partner it can count on in addressing them."
The forum, themed "The Next 50 Years: Navigating Global Transitions in an AI World", was jointly organized by the Chinese Mission to the EU, Brussels-based think tank Friends of Europe and the China Public Diplomacy Association.
Cai said China-EU relations had maintained steady momentum despite challenges. According to Chinese statistics, bilateral trade reached $693.6 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 12.9 percent year-on-year, while two-way investment stock exceeded $290 billion.
He highlighted the progress achieved at the recent second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism, where the two sides reached 16 deliverables and understandings covering trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights and World Trade Organization reform.
The two sides agreed to hold the third meeting in March next year.
"The agreement on these 16 deliverables and understandings fully demonstrates that both sides have the willingness, capability, and wisdom to resolve issues through dialogue and consultation," Cai said.
Turning to artificial intelligence, Cai said China and the EU possessed distinct strengths and should expand exchanges and cooperation to make AI a new growth area in bilateral relations while jointly advancing global AI governance.
Stefano Grassi, director for external relations at the European Commission's Secretariat-General, highlighted the deep economic ties between China and the EU, noting that China was the EU's third-largest trading partner while the EU is the first export destination for China.
Drawing on his experience during the eurozone debt crisis, Grassi said one of the most important lessons Europe had learned was that correcting economic imbalances required action from both surplus and deficit economies.
He stressed that China and the EU were highly integrated economically, and underscored the importance of jointly addressing economic challenges.
Wu Haitao, vice-president of the China Public Diplomacy Association, also emphasized the importance of dialogue in shaping the next 50 years of China-EU relations.
"Despite our differences, we are all willing to resolve them through dialogue and consultation. This is a very good starting point," Wu said, adding that "differences are inevitable, but how we resolve them matters greatly to both sides".
Against a backdrop of growing geopolitical uncertainty, Wu called on the two sides to play a constructive role in global affairs. "As two major constructive forces in the world, China and the EU should provide stability and certainty to a world marked by turbulence and change," he said.
Cai said China's commitment to high-quality development and high-standard opening-up would create new opportunities for European businesses and other international partners, expressing confidence that joint efforts would help usher in a brighter future for China-EU relations.

articles.title_orig: Russian forces launch missile attack on Ukrainian capital Kyiv, mayor says
articles.title_zh: Russian forces launch missile attack on Ukrainian capital Kyiv, mayor says
articles.content_orig:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Missile explosions struck Kyiv and left at least five people injured early on Saturday as Ukraine prepared for new talks next week with Russia and the United States.
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war. The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, following the most recent round in Geneva in February.
Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.
The Russian missiles that hit the Ukrainian capital overnight damaged homes and commercial properties, closed traffic on a Kyiv bridge over the Dnipro River and triggered new power and water outages, national and city authorities said.
“As a result of the enemy’s night attack, energy facilities in the Kyiv and ... Zhytomyr regions were damaged,” Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. “The situation with the capital’s energy supply is extremely difficult, affecting the city’s heating and water supply systems.”
Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued in the village of Komyshuvakha, devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid.
Dozens of people remain missing after 55 were killed — two of the bodies were recovered early Saturday — in the attack on the former school turned aid distribution center.
The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq, S&P 500 and AI Stocks Rebound After Brutal Week
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq, S&P 500 and AI Stocks Rebound After Brutal Week
articles.content_orig:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.
Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
Pierre BaquÃ©, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.
"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.
"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

articles.title_orig: New Zealanders head to polls on final day of voting
articles.title_zh: New Zealanders head to polls on final day of voting
articles.content_orig:
Polls have opened on the final day of voting in New Zealand against a backdrop of concerns over the rising cost of living and the broader state of the economy.
Polling stations opened at 9am on Saturday (20:00 GMT Friday) and close at 7pm (06:00 GMT Saturday).
Voting already began on October 26. More than 1.6 million voters, out of nearly 3.8 million in total, had cast their ballots by the end of Thursday, according to the country’s Electoral Commission.
The country has strict laws banning any talk of politics on election day.
The 19-hour election day blackout, which ends when polling places close on Saturday evening, bars everyone, including political parties, news outlets and social media users, from commenting on likely election outcomes, campaign issues and anything else that might encourage or discourage people from voting in a particular way.
Billboards and advertising must be removed. Bumper stickers, T-shirts and even social media profile pictures are also covered by the law.
Breaches of the law can incur a fine of up to 20,000 New Zealand dollars ($11,000).
Opinion polls ahead of the tightly contested election suggest the governing centre-right National Party and the opposition centre-left Labour Party neck and neck, with neither on course to win enough seats to govern alone.
New Zealand’s Electoral Commission aims to release preliminary results from 95 percent of polling stations by the end of election night on Saturday. A final result, which will reflect ballots cast by New Zealanders abroad, is expected by November 27.
Most parties are campaigning on the economy, but their suggested solutions differ widely.
The National Party is pledging to return the budget to surplus through fiscal discipline while expanding the national pension scheme.
The Labour Party is focusing on the cost of living, promising cheaper healthcare and transport.
Recent polls show no clear winner. A handful of seats either way could decide who governs.
New Zealand holds a general election every three years under a mixed-member proportional system.
Voters do not elect a leader of the country but instead select a local electorate candidate and a political party.
Electorate winners earn a seat in the typically 120-seat parliament, as do the highest-ranked members of the party based on their national party vote.

articles.title_orig: US urges China to honour Busan trade deal commitments
articles.title_zh: US urges China to honour Busan trade deal commitments
articles.content_orig:
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to urge Beijing to immediately implement commitments under the Busan trade agreement.
“Secretary Bessent emphasised the importance of China fully and immediately implementing its commitments made in Busan and raised concerns about recent Chinese actions. He underscored that continued progress depends on concrete results and that the United States will closely assess China’s implementation of the arrangement,” the US Department of the Treasury said in a statement announcing the discussions on Friday.
The announcement refers to a trade deal negotiated between Washington and Beijing in which US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to ease tariffs and lift restrictions on tech to de-escalate tensions amid tit-for-tat tariffs imposed first by Washington and then by Beijing.
On Thursday, China said it was open to buying more US farm goods if the world’s two largest economies agreed to implement the reciprocal tariff cut.
“China has consistently been open to expanding purchases of agricultural products from the US, but only on the condition that the two sides implement their agreed ’30 billion for 30 billion’ reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement,” Chinese Ministry of Commerce spokesperson Huang Ling said in a statement.
The move follows a September meeting between Trump and Xi, when the White House proposed $60bn in cuts, including $17bn worth of US farm goods.
In May, the White House said Beijing agreed to buy $17bn of US agricultural goods annually from 2026, with this year’s target adjusted on a prorated basis. Those purchases were in addition to a commitment made last October to buy US soya beans.
“Secretary Bessent reiterated the Trump Administration’s commitment to pursuing trade and economic policies that benefit American workers, farmers, and businesses and strengthen U.S. economic and national security,” the Treasury added.

articles.title_orig: A Retiree Who Bought 1,000 Oracle Shares at $39 Just Watched Microsoft Walk Away
articles.title_zh: A Retiree Who Bought 1,000 Oracle Shares at $39 Just Watched Microsoft Walk Away
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Microsoft is winding down an AI computing rental deal with Oracle. The stock hit a one-year low of $109.21, then closed up 0.8% at $116.10.
A retiree's 1,000 shares, bought for $39,090 in 2016, are worth $116,100, down from $328,330 at the September 2025 peak.
Selling 300 shares would cut Oracle from 12.7% to 8.9% of the portfolio for about $3,465 in federal tax.
Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)
Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) shareholders got one more piece of bad news on Friday. Bloomberg reported that Microsoft is winding down a deal to rent artificial intelligence computing capacity from Oracle, after declining to renew the contract. Oracle stock fell as low as $109.21, down 5.2% from Thursday's close and its lowest price in more than a year. Then buyers stepped in, and the stock finished the day up 0.8% at $116.10.
That bounce does little for anyone who has owned Oracle for a while. The stock closed at $328.33 on Sept. 10, 2025. At Friday's close it was 64.6% below that peak, 40.7% lower for the year and 11.2% lower for the week alone.
Take a 66-year-old retiree who bought 1,000 shares on Nov. 7, 2016, at $39.09 a share, a $39,090 investment. Those shares were worth $328,330 at the peak. On Friday they were worth $116,100. They also collect $2,700 a month from Social Security and hold another $800,000 in retirement savings, so Oracle is now 12.7% of a $916,100 portfolio. The question in front of them is whether this week's news is a reason to sell.
The deal dates to 2023. Oracle agreed to provide Microsoft with server capacity to power a new AI-assisted version of the Bing search engine. According to Bloomberg, Microsoft has been switching that rented capacity off in recent months because the older-generation chips inside Oracle's hardware no longer fit its needs. The full size of the deal was never disclosed.
If you've saved over $1,000,000, this guide is for you. The last thing you want in retirement is to run out of money, you want your money to generate lasting income while you enjoy your life.
Now you can learn the strategies wealthy retirees use to fund their retirement with The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income from Fisher Investments. Download the guide today! (sponsor)
Oracle did not deny the report. A company spokesperson said demand for its AI cloud infrastructure "remains strong," including for earlier-generation chips, and Oracle said in September that it was renewing contracts for four-year-old chips at a 20% premium to the original price.
The report landed in a week that had already been rough for Oracle shareholders:
Monday, Nov. 2: the stock fell 8.8% after Oracle announced plans to raise $20 billion, half through new stock and half through bonds.
Thursday, Nov. 5: it fell another 6.9% as artificial intelligence stocks sold off across the market.
Friday, Nov. 6: it fell as much as 5.2% on the Microsoft report, then recovered to close up 0.8%.
Measured from the purchase, the investment still looks good. The 1,000 shares cost $39,090 and are worth $116,100, a gain of $77,010, or 197%. Oracle has also paid $12.85 a share in dividends since that purchase, or $12,850 on 1,000 shares. Today it pays 50 cents a share each quarter, $2,000 a year on this position, a yield of 1.72% at Friday's price.
Measured from the peak, the same shares have given back $212,230. That is the number that keeps most long-term holders up at night, and it is the wrong one to anchor on. The $328,330 was never cash. The decision in front of this retiree is about the $116,100 that exists today.
Oracle's business is still growing quickly. In its most recent quarter, revenue rose 30% to $19.3 billion and cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121% to $7.4 billion. Its backlog of signed contracts reached $664 billion.
The stock is also far cheaper than it was. At $116.10, Oracle trades at about 18 times its earnings over the past year and about 15 times what analysts expect it to earn next year. Of the 43 analysts tracked, 35 rate it a buy or strong buy, and their average price target is $235.46, about double Friday's close.
Warren Buffett's oldest rule applies here. He has quoted his teacher Benjamin Graham for decades: "Price is what you pay; value is what you get." A stock that has fallen 65% can be a better value than it was at the top, if the business behind it is still sound.
The worries are about how Oracle is paying for its growth. The company spent $55.7 billion on equipment and data centers in its 2026 fiscal year, its total debt has reached $167 billion, and analysts expect it to burn more cash than it brings in through its 2028 fiscal year. The $20 billion raise this week added more stock and more debt on top of that.
The backlog is also concentrated. According to S&P, a single AI customer accounts for about half of the $664 billion. Microsoft's decision is small next to that, but it shows that customers can and do walk away from AI computing deals that no longer fit.
For a retiree, one stock at 12.7% of everything they own is a large bet. A further 50% drop would cost about $58,000, which is almost two years of the $32,400 Social Security pays them.
Selling part of the position is a reasonable option for this retiree. If they sell 300 of the 1,000 shares at Friday's price:
Taxable gain: $23,103, since each share cost $39.09
Federal tax at the 15% long-term rate: about $3,465
What remains: 700 shares worth $81,270, or 8.9% of the portfolio, still paying $1,400 a year in dividends
If the shares sit in a traditional IRA instead of a taxable account, there is no tax on the sale itself, and the trim costs nothing today.
That keeps most of the upside if the analysts are right and cuts the damage if this week turns out to be the start of something worse. It also turns a portion of a paper gain into cash, which is the gain that actually pays bills.
Microsoft walking away from an Oracle AI deal is a real headline, and the stock's quick recovery on Friday shows the market did not treat it as a disaster. For a 66-year-old who turned $39,090 into $116,100 over 10 years and collected $12,850 in dividends along the way, the bigger question is how much of their retirement should ride on one company. Selling 300 shares would cut Oracle to 8.9% of the portfolio for about $3,465 in tax, and the remaining 700 shares would keep paying $1,400 a year.

articles.title_orig: US Treasury sanctions Canadian money services firms over Iran-related transactions
articles.title_zh: US Treasury sanctions Canadian money services firms over Iran-related transactions
articles.content_orig:
The United States government has announced sanctions against several Canadian currency-exchange businesses accused of helping the Iranian regime and, in several cases, also helping the alleged head of a drug trafficking ring.
The U.S. Department of the Treasury on Friday said eight Canadian businesses had helped Iranian entities get around financial sanctions. It said some also helped launder proceeds of crime by changing Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets, like crypto.
"Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies," Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wrote in a statement.
Toronto businessman accused in U.S. of helping Iran's regime was also investigated in Canada
The sanctions effectively cut the Canadian firms off from the U.S. dollar-based financial system, blocking any assets ​the firms might have south of the border and banning any ​transactions with American people or entities.
In its statement, the treasury said the crackdown is part of a wider effort to "sever the economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime" and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which is listed as a terrorist organization in Canada .
The Treasury identified the sanctioned businesses in Ontario and British Columbia as the following:
The statement said the companies gave the Iranian regime "financial lifelines" by providing their services. In several cases, officials said the businesses have changed their names and addresses to avoid detection.
In August, the Trump administration expanded secondary sanctions its government can impose on ‌entities and countries maintaining business connections with Iran, raising the economic pressure on Tehran as the war neared its six-month mark.
"​Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran ⁠stands alone," Bessent said at the time.
Trump administration expands U.S. sanctions on Iran targeting countries with business ties to Tehran
In addition, the statement said three of those businesses helped Ryan Wedding — the Olympian-turned-alleged-drug-kingpin — hide money by laundering bulk cash into digital assets. Ultimately, the treasury said companies sent millions of dollars worth of digital funds abroad before Wedding was arrested in January .
CBC News has contacted Wedding's lawyer for comment.
Ryan Wedding’s path from Olympian to wanted fugitive
Rhianna Schmunk is a senior writer covering domestic and international affairs at CBC News. Her work over the past decade has taken her across North America, from the Canadian Rockies to Washington, D.C. She routinely covers the Canadian courts, with a focus on precedent-setting civil cases. You can send story tips to rhianna.schmunk@cbc.ca.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo XIV, who had cancer surgery just weeks ago, begins grueling South American tour
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo XIV, who had cancer surgery just weeks ago, begins grueling South American tour
articles.content_orig:
ABOARD THE PAPAL FLIGHT — Three countries in 12 days, a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and nine Masses on a trip covering around 19,000 miles. Less than a month after Pope Leo XIV underwent cancer surgery , he set off on what the Vatican called a “homecoming” tour of South America.
The 71-year-old’s long trip across the strongly Catholic region will take him to Uruguay and Argentina, as well as to Peru, where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023.
Leo considers the tour, one of the most grueling undertaken by a Catholic leader in decades, a “homecoming to places where he spent a long time and to which he feels closely connected,” Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni told journalists at a briefing Tuesday.
The Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, told pilgrims at his weekly audience in St. Peter’s Square on Wednesday that he was ⁠hoping to “strengthen the faith, renew hope” and “rekindle the fire of charity.”
Leo will hold several meetings with survivors of sexual abuse by ​Catholic clergy during the trip, the Vatican has said, without yet providing further details.
Bruni said the pope would also address a range of issues facing the continent, including environmental destruction, ⁠arms trafficking and regional political instability, bringing “a message of communion and unity.”
Leo departed from Rome’s Fiumicino Airport early ​Friday, and arrived in Uruguay on Friday afternoon for the country’s first papal visit since 1988.
After takeoff, Leo told journalists aboard the plane that he had no doubt he would embark on the trip.
“I know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place. I confess that from the first day I had no doubt,” he said. “I was convinced that this trip had to go forward and very happy to say, praise the Lord and thanks to wonderful medical assistants, I am here today, I think, in fairly good shape.”
Asked if he had any advice for other people facing cancer, Leo replied, “Not to be afraid, early detection is obviously the best way to go, regular check ups and take care of yourself.”
Leo also noted that “trust in God, good doctors, good surgeons, and, overall, a healthy lifestyle” had contributed to his quick recovery.
Leo, who is the first pope to vote in a U.S. election, was also asked about the importance of voting.
“I am proud to be an American and to exercise my right,” he said.
Considered the most secular country in the region, where only a fraction of people go to Mass regularly, Uruguay was the first in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use and the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion.
In October 2025, the country of just 3.5 million people became the first in the region to approve legislation for assisted dying despite strong opposition from the Catholic Church.
After Uruguay, Leo’s tour will take him to Argentina for three days, where he is expected to meet with right-wing President Javier Milei , a close ally of President Donald Trump .
It will be the first papal visit to Argentina since Pope John Paul II traveled to the country in 1987.
Leo’s immediate predecessor, Pope Francis, was born in Argentina, the first pontiff from the region, but he declined numerous invitations to return to his homeland.
The biggest crowds of the trip are likely next week during his six-day visit to Peru, where Leo is widely celebrated as a beloved national figure. He will stop off in the capital, Lima, before visiting his former diocese of Chiclayo, where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until taking up a Vatican post in 2023.
Leo, who was treated last month for lung ‌adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, will also make several high-altitude visits in the Peruvian Andes.
Doctors have ⁠said that the disease was localized and that he would not require any further treatments; Bruni said Leo had recovered enough that no additional medical measures ⁠would be necessary during his trip.
Speaking at the same briefing Tuesday, Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief, said Leo was grateful for the concern about his health and the demands the journey might make on him.
But, she said, he was “so excited” to make the trip.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Russian ballistic missiles slam Kyiv after Zelensky warns of mass attack
articles.title_zh: Russian ballistic missiles slam Kyiv after Zelensky warns of mass attack
articles.content_orig:
Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Several waves of Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv overnight on Nov. 6-7, just hours after President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia was preparing another large-scale infrastructure attack.
At least two people in the city of Kyiv have been wounded, along with a third victim in the surrounding region, according to authorities.
As Ukraine's Air Force warned that ballistic missiles were bound for the capital, a series of explosions rocked the city, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
The first barrage of missiles attacked Kyiv in quick succession, with the Air Force reporting that at least six missiles were launched at the city in the span of a few minutes shortly before 11 p.m. local time on Nov. 6.
Residents received an all-clear signal about 30 minutes later. But the respite was brief, with another aerial alert coming shortly before midnight. A fresh missile wave targeted the city shortly after 1 a.m., with Kyiv Independent journalists reporting another round of at least six loud blasts.
At least two people have been injured, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration. The victims are receiving medical treatment.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported explosions in the suburbs and warned that Russia was attacking infrastructure facilities with ballistic missiles.
Later, the mayor reported damage to a five-story residential building in the city's Solomianskyi district and shattered windows at another five-story building at an unspecified location. Emergency services have been dispatched to both scenes, he said.
A fire also broke out at a non-residential building in the Solomianskyi district, the Kyiv City Military Administration said . A kindergarten in the same district was also damaged by the attack.
Explosions again rocked the city at 3:04 a.m. local time, a Kyiv Independent journalist on the ground reported.
The wave of explosions continued with ballistic missiles targeting the city at 3:30 a.m. local time, a reporter said.
The full extent of the consequences is not yet clear. Attacks remain ongoing at the time of publication.
Outside of the city, Kyiv Oblast Governor Tymur Tkachenko reported that a Russian jet-powered drone attack in the Brovary district caused a fire in a home, injuring one victim. The man was extracted from the rubble of the damaged building and has been hospitalized due to burns and multiple shrapnel wounds.
Earlier in the evening, Zelensky told Ukrainians that intelligence reports point to another massive Russian strike on infrastructure. The attack will likely target bridges, energy facilities, and civilian infrastructure, he warned.
Kyiv, a city the size of Berlin with a population of 3 million, has come under relentless assault in recent weeks as Russia begins its annual campaign against Ukraine's power grid. The city endured the largest strike on energy this year on Nov. 3, leading to widespread blackouts and water supply cutoffs.
As residents suffer, city officials and the central government have traded blame for the worsening state of Kyiv's energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
Ukraine struck various sites in the Russian regions of Oryol, Saratov, and Rostov, hitting an oil refinery among several targets overnight on Nov. 7, monitoring channels reported.
At least three people have been injured in the city and the surrounding region. Damage has been reported at homes, apartment buildings, and a kindergarten.

articles.title_orig: To Cross the Red Sea, Shippers Email Houthi Rebels. Read Their Inbox.
articles.title_zh: To Cross the Red Sea, Shippers Email Houthi Rebels. Read Their Inbox.
articles.content_orig:
Captains who wish to transit the Bab al-Mandab Strait have been using a communication channel with the Iran-backed Houthi terror group via email for safe transit, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday.
While technically the Houthis have said ships not linked to the US, UK, or Israel are allowed through the strait, after the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in July, shippers have begun emailing the terror group to receive assurances of their safety.
Emails are sent to an administrative entity established by the Houthis in early 2024 called the Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center, which handles applications and communicates the Houthis actions.
Emails seen by the WSJ show vessels stating that neither the ship nor the crew has any connections with Israel, the US, or the UK.
Ships will share their estimated schedules and assure that they will adhere to the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea.
If the Houthis reply, they will typically do so within the next 24 hours, the WSJ wrote, citing crew members and emails.
In one instance, the Houthis sent authorization to the Chinese containership Zhong Cheng Chang Ling, issuing it a one-week permit and telling it to keep its Automatic Identification System, which broadcasts a ship's identity, position, speed, and destination, in operation through transit.
Additionally, the ship was told to keep VHF Channel 16, a marine VHF radio frequency designated as an international distress frequency, in operation.
The email ends with an invitation to call the HOCC hotline number if needed and to subscribe to the HOCC email alert service to receive news and updates from the Houthis.
The official guidance from international maritime authorities is that vessels should not engage or register with the HOCC, and many vessels choose not to contact them, the WSJ wrote.
However, the captain of the Zhong Cheng Chang Ling told the WSJ that the ship management told him to contact the Houthis as an extra precaution.
